stands_out.point: It acts on sessions that are between turns, where CachedAttention has no signal: AAS can stage a session's SSD-resident context before its next turn arrives.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CachedAttention (CA) describes only one disk-to-DRAM prefetch trigger: a waiting job inside its head-anchored look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs. It makes no prediction of when a session's next turn will arrive and treats requests as arriving randomly. Our inference from the fetch rule: a disk fetch cannot start before the job is inside the first Lpw queue positions, so its lead time is bounded by queueing delay. In agentic serving most live sessions are between turns, and restores that start at arrival come in bursts and queue up on the SSD.
stands_out.evidence: Average requests in flight, re-computed from /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/compare_20260922_023714/turns_three_tier_to.csv and the campaign-10 equivalent: 10.8 of 128 sessions at x70, and 14.3 of up to 80 in campaign 10. So 82-92% of live sessions have no queued job. At x10/x1 the figure is 85-97 of 128, so there a queue-only policy does see most sessions. At x70 the fork fetches at enqueue, which is roughly CA's trigger because the ~814K-token prefetch budget never filled. It lacks CA's demotion order and has a single FIFO reader. Under it, SSD restores were 19.6-19.7% (to) and 18.6% (wc) of returning turns, at mean TTFT 5.18 / 5.57 s. Of that, 3.01 / 4.43 s (58% / 80%) was waiting behind other reads. The reader was idle 73-77% of the read span, yet 10-s demand peaked at 4.09 / 3.94 GiB/s against a 1.88 GiB/s SSD. Every L3-hit gap was at least 46.9 s, so lead time exists. Simulation with true arrival times and EDF reads: a 10 s lead hides 81-91% of fetch time, and a 20 s lead cuts mean returning TTFT from 1.94 to 1.17 s (-40%, to) and from 1.48 to 0.50 s (-66%, wc). At realistic cadence (campaign 10) the same lever is worth only about 0.6 s on about 2.6% of turns. Agentic prior work already restores DRAM->HBM ahead of predicted returns, so the new part is doing it from a contended SSD with a queue-wait term.

stands_out.point: The fetch lead is measured in seconds and sized by SSD bandwidth plus the read backlog, with reads served earliest-deadline-first. CA's windows are job counts sized by capacity.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CA's prefetch window (Cmem/Skv jobs) and eviction window ((Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs) have no time, disk-bandwidth or read-backlog term. The paper also does not say in what order disk misses inside the window are served. On a contended SSD a fetch must start early enough to clear the reads queued ahead of it. One transfer time ahead is not enough; that is the lead used by the agentic DRAM->HBM restore schemes we reviewed. Neither is a capacity-sized number of jobs.
stands_out.evidence: x70 simulation with true arrival times: leading each read by only its own transfer time hides 16-24% of fetch time, while a 10 s lead that covers the backlog hides 81-91%. A simulation of a single FIFO reader reproduces the observed I/O completion times (median error -0.029 s). While requests waited, the reader was busy with other reads 99.5-99.7% of the time, and s2h reads overlapped 4/960 and 0/837 times. Parking cost grows with time, not with jobs. Applying the observed L2 survival curve, staged pages are re-evicted 0.8-1.2% of the time at a 10 s lead, 4.9-7.3% at 20 s and 56-64% at 60 s (model). At x1, a capacity-sized window such as the fork's budget of ~40 restores would park ~110 s of work at 0.362 admissions/s, close to one L2 turnover (~131-145 s). Not yet shown: that the explicit backlog model beats a fixed 10-20 s lead, or that EDF beats FIFO. The two give the same order when every read starts at arrival under FCFS.

stands_out.point: A cross-regime measurement of why tiering decided at arrival time fails on agent traces. CA's evaluation could not show this.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CA was evaluated on ShareGPT with Poisson session arrivals. It describes no model of time between turns and reports neither queue depth nor fetch lead time. Our runs show that the failure mode depends on the gap scale, and that the cache policy itself shapes the load regime. Any design claim has to rest on this evidence.
stands_out.evidence: x70: SSD restores are dominated by the read backlog (see above). At the same load, mean returning TTFT is 61.0 s for hbm_host against 1.94 / 1.48 s with the SSD tier. x10/x1: 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that was in L1+L2 when the request arrived. The loss grows with server wait (x1: 0% under 10 s, 29-35% at 20-30 s, at least 94% beyond 60 s). Re-computed per 10-minute window: x1 throughput falls from 3.09 turns/s, with 10% of prompt tokens uncached, in the first 10 min to 0.62 turns/s (64% uncached) in minutes 10-20 and 0.21 turns/s (79% uncached) by minutes 120-130. Prompts also grow over that time. Campaign 10 at realistic cadence shows neither failure, and every SSD restore followed a human pause of 7.7-33 min. Caveats: single seed (the to and wc arms act as rough replicates); x10/x1 server queues were shaped by the 100-connection client cap; the dense-regime failure is partly specific to our fork.

stands_out.point: Misprediction is bounded by design and quantified: predict a low quantile of the gap, fall back to fetching at arrival, re-match and re-query L3 at admission, and choose load or recompute by cost.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CA does not predict, so it has nothing to mispredict. It also does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched. A design that fetches before arrival has to show that being wrong is cheap, and the cost asymmetry shows which direction to err in.
stands_out.evidence: x70 simulation: over-estimating the gap by 25% or more keeps only 0-1% of the gain, which just reverts to today's fetch-at-arrival behaviour. Under-estimating by 25% with a 2 s margin still keeps 85-88% (by 50%: 55-63%). Predictors based on session history land within ±25% for only 34-50% of L3-hit turns, keep 54-71% of the gain, and add 500-700 GiB of SSD reads (+28-45%). The fallback is needed. The fork never re-queries L3 at admission: check_prefetch_progress returns True when no prefetch is in progress (unified_radix_cache.py:1903-1905, re-checked at HEAD 81124a061), and _prefetch_after_device_hit_loss does not exist in the fork. In the x70 to arm, 64 reads (98 GiB) were aborted after waiting 7.42 s on average, and those turns were then recomputed at 10.41 s mean TTFT. The admission re-query itself is upstream SGLang #39283/#40042 and is not new; our contribution is the error-asymmetry study.

stands_out.point: Page-level residency over a radix tree with a shared prefix, plus a GPU tier that persists across turns. Both are inherited from SGLang HiCache. A restore fetches only the pages missing from GPU and host memory.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CA's smallest unit for eviction and fetching is one session's whole KV. It reuses KV only within a session and describes no prefix tree or sharing across sessions; it mentions RadixAttention and ChunkAttention only as concurrent work. Its HBM holds the execution buffer plus read/write buffers, not a cache that persists across turns. With whole-session items, every session would re-read and re-store the shared system prompt.
stands_out.evidence: SSD restores read about 70% of the prompt: 20.3K of 29.1K tokens (x70 to), 20.5K of 28.9K (wc), 19.1K of 27.8K (campaign 10). Whole-session items would read about 1.4x the bytes, on an SSD already 2.1x oversubscribed at 10-s peaks. Storing the 7,808-token shared prompt once per session would take about 1.0M tokens, roughly 61% of the 1.63M-token L2 (arithmetic). The GPU tier serves 96% of returns after gaps under 1 min (89% of campaign-10 turns) at about 0.355 s, and host hits cost only about 26-84 ms more at p50. CA's all-or-nothing premise does hold for private context: 97.3% of replies are followed by a turn that reuses the whole previous context. That is why AAS predicts per session but stages per page. This is a difference in the underlying engine, not something AAS contributes.

stands_out.point: It addresses capacity problems that CA avoids by design: L1/L2 inclusion under write-through (handled by mirror reclaim and Â-aware demotion) and SSD write amplification.
stands_out.why_it_matters: With a GPU cache that persists across turns plus write-through, every hot context is duplicated in host memory and every page is written to the SSD. In CA, HBM is not a cross-turn tier and KV reaches disk only when evicted from host memory, so CA never runs into this. How many returns fall to the SSD or to recompute depends on unique capacity, not only on timing.
stands_out.evidence: About 40% of L2 (636-656K tokens) mirrors L1 in all 9 runs, so unique L1+L2 capacity is 1.63M tokens, not 2.30M. The idle part of the mirror is 28.7-30.6% of L2 at x70 but only 3.0-6.7% at x10/x1. A session-level LRU model predicts that mirror reclaim alone would cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5% (model, not measured). An inclusive L3 also has an upside that CA may lack. At x70, host evictions were 21.8M tokens (to) / 19.1M (wc), but only 5.27M / 3.57M were written to the SSD. That is because 18.1M / 17.2M of those tokens had been read back from the SSD and still had their SSD copy (re-computed from events_three_tier_*.csv). CA does not say whether the disk copy is kept after a fetch.

stands_out.point: A single time key (Â) ranks sessions in a gap and queued sessions together, for fetching, protection and eviction.
stands_out.why_it_matters: CA does not specify the eviction order among sessions with no queued job. Its Fig. 9 walkthrough implies, without saying so, that they are demoted before queued ones. AAS gives them an order and a protection horizon.
stands_out.evidence: Under FCFS admission, ignoring requests skipped while their fetch runs, Â = now + p/μ̂ rises with queue position. A session in a gap will join at the queue tail, so its Â is later than that of every session queued now. AAS's eviction order is therefore CA's implied order (sessions with no queued job first, then queued sessions from the tail) plus a rule among sessions in a gap. Human pauses are heavy-tailed (campaign 10: p50 84 s, p90 1,236 s), so recency already approximates the expected remaining gap; this is reasoning, not a measurement. A duration predictor therefore adds little over LRU for that ordering, while a per-turn signal such as 'tool call' versus 'handed back to the human' can. The key only differs from CA's job-order windows under non-FCFS admission (lpm, working-set admission control), which is untested.

overlaps.point: Keep every session's KV across turns in host DRAM plus SSD and reuse it on the next turn instead of recomputing it.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: AttentionStore (host memory plus disks) saves the KV caches of all requests and fetches them back when the same session becomes active again. Our data supports the idea: at x70, mean returning TTFT is 61.0 s for hbm_host and 97.0 s for GPU-only, against 1.94 / 1.48 s with the SSD tier.

overlaps.point: Decide placement from the scheduler's knowledge of upcoming work, not from LRU/FIFO history.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: Its fetching and eviction both read the scheduler's job queue, which holds full knowledge of waiting jobs. It rejects LRU and FIFO because they rely only on past accesses: 86% hit rate against 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO at 128 GB DRAM / 10 TB SSD, with fetching and eviction ablated together. For queued sessions under FCFS, AAS's Â = now + p/μ̂ contains the same information as queue position.

overlaps.point: Fetch disk-resident KV for queued requests before they run.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: A look-ahead prefetching window covers the first Lpw = Cmem/Skv waiting jobs from the head of the queue. Any of those jobs whose KV is on disk has it prefetched into host memory before the job runs. AAS's dense-regime rule (re-resolve against the SSD about 1-2 positions before the head at x1) is the same idea with the window sized in time.

overlaps.point: Evict first the content that will be needed last.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: When demoting from DRAM to disk, the item nearest the tail of the look-ahead eviction window gets higher priority, and the scan runs from tail to head. The Fig. 9 walkthrough first checks whether every DRAM-resident KV has a queued job, which implies, though the paper never spells it out, that sessions without one are demoted first. For queued sessions, AAS's 'latest Â first' gives the same order, and under FCFS every session still in a gap ranks behind every queued one.

overlaps.point: Protect the sessions about to run, within a capacity budget.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: Items whose job is inside the (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv eviction window are exempt from being evicted out of AttentionStore. That exemption covers only dropping from the store, not demotion. Tail-first demotion keeps sessions near the head of the queue in DRAM. AAS's protection (a soft priority class with budget β·(L2 − mirror − reserve), shrinking H to the earliest Â) is the same window expressed in bytes and seconds. Our L3 never dropped anything (0 cleanups), so the loss we measured happens in L2, which is exactly what CA's demotion order addresses.

overlaps.point: The session as the unit of prediction.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: One item holds all of a session's KV and is the smallest unit for eviction and fetching, because a session's KV is either all used or none of it is. AAS's registry predicts per session for the same reason (97.3% of replies are followed by a turn that reuses the whole previous context), though it stages individual pages.

overlaps.point: Keep KV saving off the critical path.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: It saves from HBM to host memory asynchronously, layer by layer, with an HBM write buffer for writes not yet finished. In a microbenchmark, asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15%. Our fork starts write-through at the last prefill chunk and chains the SSD write after the host write is acknowledged (p50 lag 0.02 s at x70).

overlaps.point: Overlap host-to-GPU loading with compute, layer by layer.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: Layer-wise pre-loading from host memory overlaps with the prefill of the new tokens. On LLaMA-13B (1K history + 100 new tokens, single GPU) it cut prefill time by 35% with no read buffer and 61% with a 15-layer buffer, both versus no pre-loading. SGLang HiCache already does the layer-wise part (LayerDoneCounter with a per-layer wait) but has no read buffer that fills before admission.

Dedicated CUDA streams move data between GPU and host, and separate IO threads move it between host and disk. The fork splits the work the same way in cache_controller threads, but with a single FIFO L3 read thread.

overlaps.point: The remedy for the dense regime.
overlaps.how_cachedattention_does_it: Both of CA's queue mechanisms target this case: tail-first demotion keeps the sessions about to run in DRAM, and window prefetch fetches the disk-resident KV of queued jobs. At x1 any policy, CA's included, must reload part of the queue from SSD, because queued private context (growing from 0.91M to 1.71-1.80M tokens) exceeds host-only L2 (at most 0.96M). No baseline faithful to CA has been run, so how much AAS gains over CA here is unknown.

cachedattention_ideas_we_lack: A bounded disk tier with a drop policy. CA's look-ahead eviction window, (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long, exempts near-future items from being evicted out of AttentionStore. When the disk is full, the KV of the last-arrived queued job outside the window is dropped (Fig. 9). Our L3 is effectively unbounded: the 70%/60% cleaner never fired and recorded 0 cleanups, while each campaign-10 SSD arm wrote about 725 GB in about 2 h. The direct translation is an L3 drop keyed on Â, with the window measured in time.

A per-session TTL counted from last access, plus a capacity-sizing method built on it. In CA's capacity study the TTL is 1 h and serves as the unit time of the capacity metric CCpUT. The hit rate is 51% at RCC/CCpUT = 0.1 and 98% at 0.25. We have no comparable rule for sizing L2 or L3 against the set of live sessions, and the live set exceeded L1+L2 in 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs.

No duplicates between HBM and host memory, and disk writes only on demotion. In CA, HBM holds only the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers, and KV reaches disk only when evicted from host memory once free memory drops to a threshold (the paper gives no value). We mirror about 40% of L2 in L1 and write every host page to the SSD. Host-to-device and host-to-SSD token counts are equal in all 6 SSD runs; about 94% of writes at x10/x1 are rewrites; each campaign-10 arm wrote about 725 GB and read about 347 GB. Caveat: at x70, writing on demotion would write about 4x more unless disk copies are kept after a fetch, which CA does not specify. So the right lesson is deduplicated, selective writes, not demotion alone.

A reserved HBM read buffer, so host-to-GPU loading can start while the previous job is still running. CA sizes it as Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew). In CA's LLaMA-13B microbenchmark, prefill time fell 35% without the buffer and 61% with a 15-layer buffer, both against no pre-loading. We have the layer-wise overlap but start loading at admission. Our host-hit penalty is only about 26-84 ms at p50, so this is low priority.

KV storage decoupled from positional encoding. CA stores K and V before positional encoding is applied and re-applies new positions at load, so saved KV can be truncated when the context overflows instead of being discarded. This needs relative positional encoding. Perplexity stays within 0.02 of recompute-based truncation, and hit rates are 17.6/41.5/18.1/18.4 points above the OF baseline. Our runs never exercised this: no replayed prompt exceeded the 131,072-token window (largest 57.6K at x70/x10/x1 and 90.6K in campaign 10), and the trace has 0 context-shrink events.
A hook that applies token-discarding lists from KV-compression methods inside the store. CA describes it but does not evaluate it.

An end-to-end cost model. CA prices GPU, DRAM and SSD time at AWS on-demand rates and reports 70/43/66/68% cost savings against recompute, with storage making up 9.0-16.4% of its cost. We report no dollar cost and no SSD-endurance cost, which matters given our write-through volume.

improvements_ranked.name: 1. Adopt CA's queue-order eviction now, and build the two fair baselines: B3 (upstream re-query) and B4 (faithful to CA)
improvements_ranked.what: Replace the current order (LRU stamps refreshed on every match) with an eviction key from the session registry. Queued sessions are ordered by FCFS position, tail evicted first. Sessions with no queued job go before queued ones, ordered by how the turn ended and then by idle time. Plain LRU applies only to nodes no session owns. Evict one session's whole private chain before touching another session's pages. Stop refreshing last_access_time when a queued request is matched at arrival. In the same pass, port upstream #39283/#40042 (L3 re-query at admission) as B3. Implement B4 faithful to CA: prefetch window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs at the head, tail-first demotion with no-queued-job sessions first (implied by CA's Fig. 9), window exemption, and whole-session items.
improvements_ranked.why: The fork evicts in the opposite order to CA. The match at arrival refreshes last_access_time (unified_tree_core.py:836-839), and LRUStrategy evicts the smallest stamp (evict_policy.py:17-18). Host eviction therefore follows arrival order and hits the requests just behind the head first. At x1 the gap between turns (p50 0.70 s) is tiny next to the server wait (p50 111 s), so removing the refresh alone still evicts the head first; the key must be queue position. Without B3 and B4 there is no evidence for any claim beyond CA. This is also the cheapest test of the Â idea, since it needs no predictor.
improvements_ranked.gain: Upper bound: the 49-55% of x10/x1 returns admitted with only the 7,808-token shared prompt cached. 93-95% of all prefill there recomputes context that was present at arrival. L2 capacity caps how much is recoverable: at x1, queued private context is 1.71-1.80M tokens against at most 0.96M of host-only L2. Some just-in-time SSD reload therefore remains, about 0.69 GiB/s or 32-37% of the SSD.
improvements_ranked.effort: Small for the key (a new EvictionStrategy that reads the registry); medium for B4; small to medium for the B3 port.
improvements_ranked.test: Run x10 and x1 (GAP=10 / GAP=1, NCONV=128, C=128, TURNS=40, OFFSET=32) without the client connection cap, with at least 3 seeds. Arms: B0, refresh removed only, tail-first key, B3, B3 + tail-first, B4. Metrics: rate of admissions with only the shared prompt cached, loss-vs-wait curve, recompute share and admissions/s per 300 s window, share of restores that mix host and storage tokens (gate: under 2%). Decision rule: if B3 + tail-first or B4 matches AAS in the dense regime, drop the dense-regime novelty claim.

improvements_ranked.name: 2. Remove the ~36 ms admission delay caused by the L3 lookup at arrival
improvements_ranked.what: When the L3 existence query for a request's unmatched suffix finds nothing, let the request be admitted in the same scheduling pass. Either wait synchronously for the query (p99 about 3 ms) or re-check prefetch progress right after check_hicache_events. Skip the query entirely when the session registry shows the suffix is new tool output beyond the session's last committed length.
improvements_ranked.why: Re-measured for this answer from campaign-10 ReqTimeStats in the server logs and /home/wanhr/sglang/agent_cache/results/compare_20260923_235624/turns_*.csv. For GPU-hit returns whose unmatched suffix is at least 256 tokens (prefetch_threshold), the server-queue wait is p50 36.0 ms (to) / 35.9 ms (wc), p90 51-52 ms. For suffixes under 256 tokens it is 1.0-1.1 ms, and in hbm_host it is 0.9 ms. The affected turns have p50 TTFT 0.332 / 0.342 s against 0.292 s in hbm_host; for suffixes under 256 tokens all arms sit at 0.231-0.236 s. This is the only measured cost of the SSD tier at realistic cadence, and it explains the previously unexplained +0.02 s paired p50 cost. It has nothing to do with CA; it is an implementation defect.
improvements_ranked.gain: About −35-40 ms on the 56.8% of returning turns whose suffix is at least 256 tokens (similar share at x70). Mean returning TTFT would go from about 0.351 to about 0.33 s (≈ −6%) at realistic cadence (estimate).
improvements_ranked.test: Run at campaign-10 cadence (lmcache_agentic_trace_262k_ge45_tl_s1.json, NCONV=283, C=80, TURNS=50, ARRIVAL=0.1), three_tier_wc vs + fix. Metrics: ReqTimeStats queue_duration by suffix bin (target about 1 ms), TTFT paired against hbm_host by suffix bin, and no loss of real restores. Pre-check without code changes: a very large prefetch_threshold in l3_extra.json should bring queue_duration down to about 1 ms (that arm loses real restores).

improvements_ranked.name: 3. Deduplicate SSD writes (skip pages L3 already holds)
improvements_ranked.what: Before backing a node up to L3, drop the pages whose hash L3 already has. Do this with batch_exists in the backup thread, or with an in-memory set or Bloom filter of acknowledged keys that the L3 cleaner invalidates. This matches the file backend's behaviour.
improvements_ranked.why: In the nixl backend, batch_set_v1 transfers every page without checking whether it already exists (/home/wanhr/sglang/python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/storage/nixl/hicache_nixl.py, batch_set_v1). The file backend skips keys already on disk (hicache_storage.py set(): 'same key already on disk ... skip rewrite'). In all 6 SSD runs, tokens copied GPU→host equal tokens written host→SSD exactly. At x10/x1, about 94% of the 54-58M tokens written are rewrites of recomputed pages the SSD already holds: about 5 TB per run, about 0.6 GiB/s at x1. About 32% of writes in the x70 to arm are rewrites after aborted reads. This is the cheap half of CA's lower write volume (CA writes to disk only when evicting from host memory) and keeps our inclusive L3, where re-evicting a page costs no new write.
improvements_ranked.gain: SSD writes −90% or more at x10/x1 and about −30% in the x70 to arm (estimate). Also better SSD endurance and more bandwidth for just-in-time reloads. In the x70 to arm, reads overlapping at least 0.3 GiB/s of write-through ran at p50 1.36 GiB/s against 3.31 GiB/s without concurrent writes (correlational).
improvements_ranked.test: x1 (GAP=1): three_tier_to vs three_tier_to_dedup. iostat wkB/s on /dev/vdc should fall to x70-like levels while host→SSD submissions stay the same. x70 (GAP=70, GAP_CAP=1200): compare the SSD→host read-bandwidth distribution and timeout aborts (64 in B0). Unit check: replay one conversation twice and assert its bytes are written only once.

improvements_ranked.name: 4. Measure the dense regime open-loop on goodput, and fill in x20-x50
improvements_ranked.what: Replace the closed loop of 128 sessions with open-loop Poisson session arrivals at 50-120% of capacity. Report admissions/s and uncached share per window, plus session makespan, with at least 3 seeds. Add gap scales x20-x50.
improvements_ranked.why: In the closed loop, mean TTFT ≈ 128 / throughput − decode − gap, so TTFT cannot show whether a fix works; throughput can. Re-computed from turns_three_tier_to.csv: x1 falls from 3.09 turns/s with 10% of prompt tokens uncached in the first 10 min, to 0.62 turns/s (64% uncached) in minutes 10-20, to 0.21 turns/s (79%) by minutes 120-130. Overall that is about 6.6K uncached tokens/s, close to the batched prefill rate of about 7.5K tokens/s. The x10/x1 queues were also shaped by the 100-connection client cap. There are no runs between x10 and x70, where the gap term Ĝ and the queue-wait term Ŵ are comparable and the single-rule claim is actually tested.
improvements_ranked.gain: Makes the dense-regime claim measurable, and finds the load at which B0, B3, B4 and AAS each start to collapse.
improvements_ranked.test: Sweep ARRIVAL ∈ {0.02, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08} sessions/s with C=256 on the 262K trace at GAP=1/10/70, then GAP=20/35/50, via run_compare.sh with CLIENT_TIMEOUT set. Plot throughput and uncached share per 300 s window and find the collapse point for each arm.

improvements_ranked.name: 5. Stage returns after human pauses from a client warm-up hint and the turn-end type, not from a duration predictor
improvements_ranked.what: At turn end, record whether the reply hands control back to the human or calls a tool, and use this in the Â key: sessions waiting on the human are ranked by the pause survival curve, sessions waiting on a tool are treated as returning soon. Add a lightweight warm(session) hint that the client sends when the user starts typing or focuses the session. It stages the session's registry chain from L3 into L2 and protects it for H. Limit hints per session, and drop protection if no request follows.
improvements_ranked.why: At realistic cadence, every turn that reaches the SSD follows a human pause. In campaign 10, restores followed gaps of 459-1,992 s (p50 1,306 s). The replayed pause is lognormal (p50 84 s, p90 1,236 s, p90/p50 ≈ 15x), so predicting the admission time from the last round of conversation cannot be accurate to within seconds. History-based predictors under-predict 98.8-99.0% of L3-hit turns. An uncontended restore fetch takes only about 0.6 s, so about 1 s of warning from a hint is enough. CA describes no think-time model and no client signal.
improvements_ranked.gain: Restored turns go from 1.01 s to about 0.43 s. At campaign-10 cadence, returning p99 goes from 1.36 s to about 1.21 s (−11%) and the mean drops about 3% (estimate). The gain is larger when many users return at once and restores contend.
improvements_ranked.effort: Small in the server; needs an API and client change
improvements_ranked.test: At campaign-10 cadence, have replay_agentic.py send the hint T_lead ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 5 s} before each turn with gap_think > 0, and set the turn-type flag at the end of the previous turn. The flag is an oracle, because the replay draws pauses independently of the reply. Arms: three_tier_wc vs + hint. Metrics: TTFT in the ≥ 10 min gap class, SSD read amplification, bytes staged for unused hints. Stress variant: 40 sessions returning within 30 s.

improvements_ranked.name: 6. Validate staging before arrival with a real predictor, starting from the simplest timing rule
improvements_ranked.what: At x70, run: FIFO fetch at arrival (B0); a fixed 10 s and 20 s lead with request-level EDF reads (a TokenCake-style lead plus margin); and the backlog-aware lead. Drive each with a per-tool low-quantile predictor, with the oracle as the ceiling. Compare at equal SSD read amplification and equal parked bytes. Keep the backlog model only if it is better on TTFT without costing more parked bytes or re-evictions. Consider ranking candidates by return hazard and staging only into idle SSD bandwidth, instead of predicting a point Â. Try chunk-level EDF only if deadline misses remain.
improvements_ranked.why: Every sparse-regime number comes from oracle arrival times on a deterministic 70x stretch of the trace. A fixed generous lead may capture nearly all of the gain: 10 s hides 81-91%, and 20 s hides about 100% with 4.9-7.3% re-eviction. EDF and FIFO give the same order when every read starts at arrival under FCFS. History predictors keep only 54-71% of the gain and add 500-700 GiB of reads. This experiment decides whether AAS's timing rule is the contribution, or simply starting earlier.
improvements_ranked.gain: If a non-oracle predictor keeps at least 70% of the oracle gain: x70 mean returning TTFT about −28% (to) and −46% (wc), i.e. 70% of the oracle's −40% / −66%, with SSD read amplification at most 1.2x.
improvements_ranked.test: x70 (GAP=70, GAP_CAP=1200, NCONV=128, C=128, TURNS=40) with gaps resampled stochastically, plus a run with the SSD throttled to 0.5x (cgroup io.max on /dev/vdc), at least 3 seeds. Metrics: storage-hit TTFT p50/p90, deadline misses (fetch finished after admission), re-eviction of staged pages, parked bytes, read amplification. Gate: no regime worse than B0.

improvements_ranked.name: 7. Stop mirroring running requests in host memory: copy to host at request finish
improvements_ranked.what: Move the GPU→host write-through of a request's prompt pages from the last prefill chunk to request finish. The pages stay locked on the GPU until the copy is acknowledged, and the SSD write is chained after it. Combine this with element 9's reclaim of idle mirrors whose SSD write is acknowledged.
improvements_ranked.why: About 39-40% of L2 mirrors L1, but the idle part of the mirror is only 3.0% (x1) and 5.9-6.7% (x10). So about 33-36% of L2 holds copies of running contexts that are locked on the GPU and unused through a mean decode of 50-54 s. CA has no such duplicates because its HBM is not a cache tier. Its lesson of saving during the job is the wrong one for us, because our L1 is a cache tier.
improvements_ranked.gain: +0.54-0.59M tokens of L2 for queued contexts at x10/x1, about +60% of host-only space. Host-only L2 would be about 1.5M tokens against about 1.59M needed to hold the whole x1 queue. About +10% of L2 at x70 (estimate).
improvements_ranked.effort: Medium. Risk: a decode that is retracted or preempted has no host copy and must be recomputed.
improvements_ranked.test: x1 and x10: three_tier_wc vs + copy at finish (with and without idle-mirror reclaim) vs write_back. Metrics: mirror size, host-only L2 occupancy, rate of admissions with only the shared prompt cached, recompute share, admissions/s, retraction count. Check for regressions at x70 and in campaign 10 (1-5 min class: 92.5% host hits).

improvements_ranked.name: 8. Choose compute or load by backlog (or split the work) instead of waiting and then aborting
improvements_ranked.what: When the fetch is issued and again at admission, compare the expected load finish time ((EDF backlog + own bytes) / BW) with recompute time at the current prefill throughput. Then recompute, load, or split the work: recompute a prefix while loading the rest, sized so both finish together (x / r_gpu = (n − x) / r_ssd).
improvements_ranked.why: In the x70 to arm, 64 reads (98 GiB) were aborted after waiting 7.42 s on average, and those turns were then recomputed at 10.41 s mean TTFT, so they paid twice. CA does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk.
improvements_ranked.gain: At x70, removes about 64 turns that each paid twice (about 5-6 s each). Under backlog, storage-hit TTFT is capped near the recompute time for a 20.3K-token restore (about 4.1 s). With no contention, a split is about 19% faster than loading alone (arithmetic).
improvements_ranked.effort: Medium (requires loading a suffix while prefilling a prefix in the radix tree)
improvements_ranked.test: x70: three_tier_to (B0) vs three_tier_cost, plus a run with the SSD throttled to 0.5x. Metrics: aborted reads, storage-hit TTFT p50/p90, GPU prefill-time share, total recomputed tokens.

improvements_ranked.name: 9. Working-set admission control keyed on Â (load control with timed SSD swap-in)
improvements_ranked.what: When the predicted live set exceeds unique L1+L2, admit only from an active set ordered by Â, FCFS within it. Parked sessions fall to L3 and rotate in by age every quantum Q, or when an active session enters a long gap. AAS stages each parked session from L3 just before its slot.
improvements_ranked.why: Here Â stops increasing with queue position, so CA's job-order windows cannot express the policy; CA describes no reordering by cache location. This is the strongest potential way to stand apart from CA. The dense runs look like a collapse that sustains itself: the server spends most of its time recomputing (about 6.6K uncached tokens/s against about 7.5K tokens/s of prefill capacity), and no ordering can hold the whole x1 queue in L2.
improvements_ranked.gain: Estimate: dense-regime throughput from 0.2-0.7 to at least about 1.4 turns/s (2-6x), with session makespan falling accordingly. In a closed loop of 128 sessions, mean TTFT falls only to about 50-85 s (Little's law). Parked sessions pay a bounded extra wait.
improvements_ranked.effort: Large; needs an aging bound and a fairness metric
improvements_ranked.test: x1 and x10 without the connection cap: three_tier_wc vs three_tier_wc_ws vs lpm vs B3. Metrics: throughput and uncached share per 300 s window, makespan p50/p95, per-session maximum TTFT, Jain's fairness index. Gate: uncached share under 10% after minute 10, and at least 2x B3's throughput.

improvements_ranked.name: 10. Bound L3 with a session-aware drop policy (CA's disk window, measured in time)
improvements_ranked.what: Cap L3. Drop ended sessions first (client closed, or final turn). Next drop sessions whose probability of returning within the horizon is below ε, given idle time so far and how the last turn ended. Then fall back to LRU. Exempt sessions whose Â falls inside a time window, as CA exempts queued jobs inside its eviction window.
improvements_ranked.why: L3 never evicted anything (0 cleanups), while each campaign-10 SSD arm wrote about 725 GB in about 2 h. A production deployment needs a drop policy. CA's window exemption plus per-session TTL is the closest published template.
improvements_ranked.gain: The L3 footprint tracks the live set instead of every context ever written: about 2-3x less SSD capacity at campaign-10 load (estimate). It also avoids a capacity-driven cleaner dropping sessions that are about to return; a wrong drop turns a ~1.0 s restore into a ~3.2 s recompute.
improvements_ranked.effort: Medium (needs a session-close API and TTL tuning)
improvements_ranked.test: At campaign-10 cadence, cap L3 at about 300 GB via L3_CLEANER_PCT and a quota on /mnt/ssd/hicache_l3, with the replay marking conversation end. Compare the stock cleaner with the session-aware cleaner. Metrics: SSD vs recompute shares in the ≥ 10 min gap class, bytes deleted, SSD hit rate.

improvements_ranked.name: 11. Give restores priority over write-through on the SSD (after a controlled fio test)
improvements_ranked.what: Treat L3 writes as background work whose deadline is the page's predicted eviction from L2. Throttle or pause backups while a read with a near deadline is queued. Bound the host bytes not yet backed up, and force a flush before eviction.
improvements_ranked.why: In the x70 to arm, per-read bandwidth fell from p50 3.31 GiB/s with under 0.05 GiB/s of concurrent writes to 1.36 GiB/s with at least 0.3 GiB/s. This is correlational, and the wc arm shows little effect. Writes have slack: L2 turns over in about 131-145 s at x10/x1 and in minutes at x70.
improvements_ranked.gain: If the effect is causal, restore I/O during x70 bursts falls 30-60%, which shrinks the lead AAS needs. Little effect at campaign-10 load (SSD at most 34% busy).
improvements_ranked.effort: Medium; interacts with the path that skips backups (unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414)
improvements_ranked.test: First run fio with O_DIRECT on /dev/vdc: 2 MiB sequential reads alone, then with 0.3 / 0.6 / 1.0 GiB/s of concurrent writes. If reads degrade, compare x70 three_tier_wc vs + write gating. Metrics: SSD→host read GiB/s by concurrent-write bin, storage-hit TTFT p50/p90, host→SSD lag, peak bytes not yet backed up.

improvements_ranked.name: 12. A CA-style read buffer for host hits, filled before admission (L2→L1)
improvements_ranked.what: While the previous batch runs, start the host→GPU load for the 1-2 requests with the earliest Â into a small reserved region of L1, as CA's HBM read buffer does.
improvements_ranked.why: CA's read buffer lets loading start while the previous job is still running: 61% vs 35% prefill-time reduction with and without a 15-layer buffer in its microbenchmark. SGLang already overlaps the load layer by layer, but only starts it at admission.
improvements_ranked.gain: At most about 30-80 ms on host-hit turns; under 1% of mean returning TTFT at campaign-10 cadence.
improvements_ranked.effort: Medium. Risk: reserving L1 shrinks batch capacity, which is the binding resource in the dense regime.
improvements_ranked.test: Campaign 10 and x70: three_tier_wc vs + staging for the queue head. Metrics: host-tier TTFT p50 by suffix bin, L1 batch size, decode throughput.

improvements_ranked.name: 13. Invalidate orphaned chains on context compaction; defer KV storage decoupled from positional encoding
improvements_ranked.what: When a session's new prompt diverges from its registry chain well before n_s (compaction, history edit, rewind), mark the orphaned chain to be evicted first from L1/L2 and delete it from L3. Do not build CA-style K storage before RoPE until a trace shows overflow or reuse of shifted segments.
improvements_ranked.why: No replayed prompt exceeded the 131,072-token window and the trace has 0 context-shrink events, so CA's decoupled truncation would never trigger. Real agent harnesses do compact context, which leaves whole chains orphaned in both designs.
improvements_ranked.gain: Frees about n_s tokens of L2/L3 per compaction. How often real agents compact is unknown.
improvements_ranked.test: Build a compaction variant of the trace with make_tl_trace.py (replace the history with a ~2K-token summary once it passes ~40K tokens) and run it at campaign-10 cadence. Metrics: orphaned bytes resident in L2/L3 over time, time until they are evicted, TTFT of the turn after compaction.

improvements_ranked.name: 14. Session-affinity routing aware of Â across instances sharing L3
improvements_ranked.what: Route a returning turn to the instance that holds its context, unless that instance's predicted admission delay costs more than restoring from the shared L3 on another instance. Feed each instance's Â and read backlog to the router, and stage the context at the target after a reroute.
improvements_ranked.why: CA does not discuss routing across instances. With data parallelism and a shared L3, which instance's admission time matters changes. Campaign-10 tier costs bound what is at stake: GPU 0.355 s, host about 0.39 s, SSD 1.02 s, recompute 3.21 s.
improvements_ranked.gain: Unknown; bounded by those per-tier costs times the misroute rate.
improvements_ranked.test: First, a trace-driven simulation using campaign-10 per-tier latencies and registry residency, comparing round-robin, sticky and Â-aware routing. Then two instances on one nixl L3 directory, if a second GPU is available.

syn.positioning: CachedAttention set the template we build on. It keeps every session's KV in host DRAM plus SSD instead of recomputing it. The scheduler's job queue, not LRU/FIFO history, decides which disk-resident KV to prefetch (a window of Cmem/Skv jobs from the queue head) and which host-resident session to demote (the one nearest the window's tail first), and it moves whole sessions. Admission-anchored staging is best described as an extension of that scheduler-aware idea into the time domain, for agentic serving on a write-through tiered engine with a radix tree ('forestall for agentic KV tiers'). It is not a new paradigm. For queued sessions under FCFS, Â = now + p/μ̂ only increases with queue position, and every session that has not yet arrived has a later Â than every queued one, so AAS reproduces CachedAttention's ordering there. The large dense-regime loss we measured, where 93-95% of prefill recomputes context that was present at arrival, mostly shows that our fork lacks CachedAttention's queue mechanisms and upstream SGLang's admission-time re-query. AAS goes beyond CachedAttention where the paper has no signal or no time term. It stages from the SSD for the 82-92% of live sessions that are between turns in our sparse and realistic runs. It sizes the lead by SSD bandwidth and read backlog: at x70, 58-80% of storage-hit TTFT is waiting behind other reads while the reader is idle about 75% of the time, and with oracle arrival times a 10-20 s lead cuts mean returning TTFT by 40-66%. It also deals with the capacity costs that CachedAttention avoids by design: with a GPU tier that persists across turns plus write-through, about 40% of L2 mirrors L1. Agentic KV work already restores DRAM to HBM ahead of predicted returns, so the defensible novelty narrows to three things: the contended SSD tier, the joint key of gap plus queue wait, and the cross-regime measurements, which are currently the strongest part. Nothing is shown end to end yet. Every AAS gain is an oracle or model estimate, no baseline faithful to CachedAttention has been run, and at realistic cadence the timing lever is worth about 0.6 s on 2.6% of turns.
risks: No baseline faithful to CachedAttention (B4) has been run, nor a port of upstream's admission-time re-query (B3, #39283/#40042), and AAS itself is not implemented. Every AAS gain is an oracle or model estimate, so 'beyond CachedAttention' currently has no measured support.

Under FCFS, AAS orders queued sessions exactly as CachedAttention does: Â increases with queue position, and sessions still in a gap always rank behind queued ones. The dense-regime prize mostly reflects defects in the fork. LRU refresh at match evicts the request about to run, tails under 256 tokens get no protection, fetched pages are unlocked on insert, and admission never re-queries L3. If tail-first eviction plus B3 recovers the loss, the dense-regime claim reduces to engineering.

Predictability. The sparse-regime headroom comes from oracle arrival times on a deterministic 70x stretch of trace gaps. History predictors keep only 54-71% of the gain and add 500-700 GiB of SSD reads (+28-45%, above the target of at most 1.2x). Per-tool quantiles are untested. At realistic cadence, the turns that reach the SSD follow human pauses (p90/p50 ≈ 15x) whose timing the last round of conversation cannot predict.

Realism. The only run at realistic cadence (campaign 10) shows neither failure mode: peak queue 3-6, SSD at most 34% busy. There the timing lever is worth about 0.6 s on about 2.6% of turns, roughly 0.016 s on the mean. The large wins come from x70, a deterministic stretch, and from x10/x1, closed loops whose server queues were shaped by a 100-connection client cap and where mean TTFT ≈ 128 / throughput.

Cheaper levers may shrink the sparse-regime prize. Mirror reclaim alone is modelled to cut x70 SSD/cold returns from 21% to 2.7-4.5%, a 4-8x smaller set of turns to fix. L3 write dedup or giving reads priority over writes could shrink the restore backlog that justifies fetching early.

Prior art narrows the novelty. Predictive restore ahead of tool returns for agents (TokenCake, Ask the Tool, KVFlow; SYMPHONY promotes across tiers on client advisories), storage prefetch hooks in production stacks, and classic prefetching theory (forestall, TIP, feedback-directed prefetching, DEMOTE) already cover the individual pieces. These descriptions of related work come from our review and were not re-verified in this pass.

Numbers across papers are not comparable. CachedAttention's 86% hit rate and over 99.6% DRAM hits come from ShareGPT with Poisson session arrivals on LLaMA/Falcon (4x A100, 128 GB DRAM, 10 TB SSD), and the paper describes no timing between turns. Our metrics are TTFT on ~29K-token agent prompts with Qwen3-30B-A3B on an H200. Any 'better than CachedAttention' statement must come from running B4 in our engine.

Rebase risk. Upstream HiRadixCache keeps staged L3 pages pinned outside the tree until the FCFS scan finalises them (#32724), and it has the admission-time re-query. The diagnoses specific to our fork (pages unlocked on insert, no re-query) must be re-checked after a rebase, and part of the measured loss may disappear.

Closed-loop shift. Once recompute stops, admission rate, queue depth and SSD demand all change. At x1, just-in-time reload (~0.69 GiB/s) plus today's write-through (~0.6 GiB/s) would use about 65-70% of the 1.88 GiB/s SSD. GPU-resident KV (668K tokens, about 24 contexts) may keep x1 queued anyway. The live set exceeds L1+L2 for 42-48% of the x10/x1 runs, so some SSD traffic is unavoidable.

Protection mechanics. A hard host lock can suppress write-through backups: _execute_kv_backup skips the backup when evict_host cannot free space (unified_radix_cache.py:1410-1414). A soft priority class may not hold under pressure. Neither has been exercised.

Measurement hygiene. Every result is a single seed, and x10 arms 1-3 lack ReqTimeStats. Small inconsistencies remain: x70 to storage restores 890 vs 896, and x70 hbm_host mean TTFT 61.0 vs 59.5 s. There are no runs between x10 and x70, the regime where the single-rule claim is actually tested.

Agent harnesses that rewrite context (compaction, history edits) would invalidate prefixes in both designs, and this is untested. CachedAttention's decoupling from positional encoding handles truncation on overflow, not rewritten history.

checks.claim: Layer-wise pre-loading overlaps loading the KV of later layers from host memory with the computation of the current layer.
checks.correction: Correct. The paper adds that the computation being overlapped is the prefill of the session's new input tokens: 'overlap the loading of the KV cache with the prefilling computation of new input tokens for the conversation.' Checked against arXiv v3, the ATC'24 camera-ready ('Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024'). The same wording is in v1.
checks.quote: "The main idea is to overlap the loading of the KV cache with the prefilling computation of new input tokens for the conversation. In particular, the LLM model is chained by multiple transformer layers, each with its own KV cache. As the GPU executes a layer, the KV cache needed by the subsequent layers can be loaded from the host memory concurrently. By doing so, when the GPU starts computing the self-attention for a layer, the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer."
checks.section: §3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs (Fig. 6b)

checks.claim: An HBM read buffer lets pre-loading start while the previous job is still running.
checks.correction: Correct. The stated reason: without the read buffer, loading cannot start until the previous job frees the HBM execution buffer, which leaves a gap before Layer 1. The read buffer removes that gap.
checks.quote: "However, a gap still exists between the last job and the first layer of the current job, since the loading can only commence once the HBM execution buffer is available, i.e., the last job is finished. To further mitigate the gap between the last job and the first layer of the current job, CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap. Specifically, as shown in Figure 6c, with the read buffer, the read stream doesn't have to wait for the release of the execution buffer from the last job. The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running."

checks.claim: The read-buffer size is set by Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew).
checks.correction: The formula is quoted correctly. Definitions: Tload is the KV access time per token, Tpref is the prefill time per token, Lhist is the number of history tokens, Lnew is the number of new input tokens, and B is the PCIe bandwidth. The formula only applies under imperfect overlap (Tload·Lhist > Tpref·Lnew). Here the paper motivates a 'customized larger pre-loading buffer' that lets loading start earlier. Some of the paper's text calls it the 'buffer' or 'pre-loading buffer' rather than 'read buffer', though the evaluation labels these sizes as read-buffer sizes.
checks.quote: "Let Tload , Tpref, Lhist and Lnew denote the access time of the KV cache for a token, the prefilling time for a token, the length of historical tokens in a session, and the length of new input tokens in the conversation, respectively. Imperfect overlapping happens when Tload Lhist > Tpref Lnew, which indicates that the transmission time is larger than the partial prefilling time. The buffer is used to fill up the time gap Tload Lhist− Tpref Lnew. Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(Tload Lhist− Tpref Lnew)."

checks.claim: With LLaMA-13B, 1K history plus 100 new tokens, pre-loading cuts prefill time by 35% with no read buffer (PL-B0) and by 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15).
checks.correction: The numbers and setup are correct. Missing context: both reductions are measured against NO-PL (no pre-loading), on a single GPU with batch size 16. The paper also says the 15-layer buffer 'perfectly overlaps' the load time. The buffer is measured in layers of KV cache. The paper's text typos the label as 'PF-B15'; Fig. 19 labels it 'PL-B15'.
checks.quote: "The model used is LLaMA-13B with a single GPU and the batch size is set to 16. Layer-wise KV cache pre-loading. We set the length of historical tokens to 1K and the length of newly input tokens to 100 ... For clarity, we use the number of layers to represent the buffer size, e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache. We observe although there is no read buffer, i.e., PL-B0, the pre-loading scheme reduces the prefilling time by 35% compared to NO-PL. PF-B15 perfectly overlaps the KV cache loading time and reduces the prefilling time by 61% compared to NO-PL."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Fig. 19)

checks.claim: Asynchronous saving writes prefill-phase KV layer by layer, overlapped with decoding, writes decode-phase KV layer by layer while decoding, and moves unfinished writes to an HBM write buffer.
checks.correction: Accurate in substance. Wording differences: for prefill, the paper says the write stream 'retains' the KV layer by layer, and that this KV 'can be overlapped with' decoding. It does not literally say 'writes'. The write buffer is described as covering the case where write-back has not finished when decoding finishes, so that the next job is not blocked. The baseline it replaces writes all KV together after the round of conversation ends.
checks.quote: "As shown in Figure 8b, for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding. To avoid getting stuck if the KV cached is not fully written back when the decoding is already finished, we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job."
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory (Fig. 8)

checks.claim: Asynchronous saving reduces total execution time by 13-15%.
checks.correction: Correct. Missing context: the 13-15% is from one microbenchmark. Settings: LLaMA-13B on a single GPU, batch size 16, prompt lengths 1K to 1.6K, and 20 decoding steps. Only 20 decode steps leaves little decode time to hide the writes. Do not cite it as a general end-to-end number.
checks.quote: "Asynchronous KV cache saving. We set different prompt lengths ranging from 1K to 1.6K and the number of decoding steps to 20 for investigating the effectiveness of the asynchronous saving scheme. As Figure 20 shows, the saving time increases as the prompt length grows, as the size of the KV cache to be saved increases. To reduce the saving overhead, CachedAttention employs the asynchronous saving scheme allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution, reducing the overall execution time by 13% to 15%."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Fig. 20)

checks.claim: The paper rejects LRU and FIFO because they rely solely on historical access information.
checks.correction: Substantively correct. The paper contrasts itself with LRU/FIFO for relying only on historical access information, and in the evaluation blames their low hit rates on lacking future-access information. Two nuances: (a) 'rejects' only means 'does not adopt'; LRU and FIFO are still used as evaluation baselines in §4.3.3. (b) The 'future access information' CachedAttention uses is only the scheduler's job queue of requests that have already arrived ('the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs', §3.3.1). It is a look-ahead window over queued jobs, not a prediction of when an idle session will return. The paper does not say how it picks among items outside the window. Verified identical in arXiv v3 (same file as the current arxiv.org/pdf/2403.19708), the USENIX ATC'24 PDF and arXiv v1 (titled AttentionStore).
checks.quote: "Different from the existing cache eviction strategies, such as the least-recently-used (LRU) [46], first-in-first-out (FIFO) [8], and their variants, which solely rely on the historical access information of the KV caches, CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate." (§3.3.2). Also §4.3.3: "This is because LRU and FIFO lack awareness of future KV cache information and cannot pre-fetch KV caches from disks to host memory, thereby limiting their ability to improve DRAM hit rates."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; §4.3.3 Scheduler-aware Fetching and Eviction

checks.claim: CachedAttention gives each session's KV a TTL measured from its last access; it appears only in the capacity-sizing analysis and is set to one hour in that experiment.
checks.correction: Correct. A full-text search of arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF finds 'TTL' / 'time to live' only in §4.3.6. The Design section (§3) never describes a TTL mechanism. One nuance: the paper also makes the TTL the 'unit time' in DSpUT/CCpUT ('The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above'). So the capacity metric CCpUT is defined per TTL window, and the TTL is part of how the paper sizes capacity, not just a parameter of the experiment. arXiv v1 has the same text, with 'AttentionStore' in place of 'CachedAttention'.
checks.quote: "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above." ... "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour."
checks.section: §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement

checks.claim: In the capacity study (TTL 1 h), the hit rate is 51% at a capacity ratio (RCC/CCpUT) of 0.1 and 98% at 0.25.
checks.correction: The numbers match the text exactly. Minor nuance: the x-axis of Figure 23 is labelled 'Storage Capacity / DSpUT', while the text calls the ratio RCC/CCpUT. In arXiv v1 the same result is Figure 25a.
checks.quote: "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour. As shown in Figure 23a, when the ratio RCC/CCpUT is 0.1, we achieve the cache hit rate of 51%. When the ratio RCC/CCpUT is 0.25, we achieve the cache hit rate of 98%."
checks.section: §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement (Figure 23a)

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, one item is all of a session's KV; this is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity, justified because a session's KV is either all used or none of it.
checks.correction: Verbatim match, and the same in arXiv v1, v3 and the USENIX version.
checks.quote: "Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: AttentionStore manages host memory and disks in blocks.
checks.correction: Correct, but it is an implementation detail about storage allocation, given in the experimental setup with a citation to vLLM [21]. checks.claim: CachedAttention (USENIX ATC '24; arXiv 2403.19708 v3) saves the KV caches of all requests in AttentionStore, a KV caching system made of host DRAM and SSDs, and reuses them for later turns of the same session.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Bibliographic check: arXiv v3 (30 Jun 2024) is the latest version and carries the comment "Accepted to USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2024". USENIX lists it in ATC '24, pp. 111-126. One caveat: "save for all requests" describes what gets written, not how long it stays. Entries can be evicted "out of the system" when disks are full (§3.3.2), and each session's KV has a TTL (§4.3.6), so later reuse depends on a cache hit (86/71/89/90% in §4.2). It is not guaranteed.

Upon the resumption of the same session, CachedAttention loads and reuses the saved KV cache from AttentionStore". §3.1: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." §3.3: "The access speed of host memory, i.e., DRAM, is much higher than disks, i.e., SSDs, (tens of GB/s v.s. several GB/s)." §4.3.6: "the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access."

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn KV cache tier.
checks.correction: Substantively correct, with three notes. (1) The paper never says in so many words that HBM is not a cache tier. The point is shown by Figure 5, where the AttentionStore box contains only Host memory and Disks and GPU0/HBM0 and GPU1/HBM1 sit outside it in the GPU Cluster, and by the §2.4 and §4.3.7 wording below. (2) The three buffers are not everything in HBM: §2.4 notes that "130 GB of HBM space is allocated to store the model", and running jobs' KV is in HBM during execution. (3) §4.3.7 has one ambiguous phrase. After an HBM+DRAM baseline it says "by further extending the cache capacity with SSDs, CachedAttention improves the cache hit rate", which could be read as that experiment's CA config keeping the 10GB HBM cache. However, the same section's framing sentence and the whole design section put CA's cache on DRAM and SSDs.
checks.quote: §3.2.1: "when the GPU starts computing the self-attention for a layer, the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer." ... "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap." §3.2.2: "we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job." §2.4: "the KV caches of historical conversations can be saved in a KV caching system out of GPUs." §4.3.7: "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs."

checks.claim: CachedAttention does not predict when a session's next turn will arrive or be admitted.
checks.correction: Correct as a negative claim. I searched the full v3 text for predict, forecast, estimat, arriv, interval, idle, inactive and TTL. Nothing predicts a session's next-turn arrival or admission time. The paper treats arrivals as random, and its evaluation draws arrivals from a Poisson distribution. Nuance: its "future access information" is the order of jobs already in the scheduler's waiting queue. It therefore knows the relative order of admissions that are about to happen for requests that have already arrived, but nothing about turns that have not arrived yet, and it never estimates a time. Cache retention beyond the queue is handled by eviction plus a fixed TTL since last access, not by any timing prediction.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks, resulting in poor access performance." ... "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed." §3.3.2: "CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate. The job queue in the job scheduler gives us the opportunity to achieve this." §4.1: "we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates"

checks.claim: CachedAttention's scheduler-aware fetching prefetches disk-resident KV into host memory for waiting jobs inside a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window over the scheduler's job queue.
checks.correction: No correction needed. "Head-anchored" is not in the text. It comes from Figure 9, where the job queue is labeled "head" at the Job 2 end. The "prefetching window, size: 2" bracket covers Job 3 and Job 2, the jobs next in line while Job 1 runs. The "eviction window, size: 6" bracket covers Job 7 through Job 2 and is also anchored at the head.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "we leverage a scheduler-aware KV cache fetching scheme to pre-fetch the KV caches to be accessed from disks to the host memory. This is done by utilizing the hints from the inference job scheduler. ... CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." ... "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3."

checks.claim: The prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs, where Cmem is the host memory available for prefetching and Skv is the average per-session KV size.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The unit ("jobs") is not written next to the formula. It follows from the Figure 9 example, where 2 host-memory KV slots give a window covering waiting Jobs 2-3. One item is one session's KV (§3.3.2), so dividing by the per-session size gives a count of jobs/sessions.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."

checks.claim: The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs, described as a maximum set by the total capacity of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The word "maximum" appears in the sentence before the formula. The formula sentence itself just says "The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv". Cmem is the term defined in §3.3.1 as "available memory capacity for prefetching", and Cdisk is "the total available capacity in the disks". In the Figure 9 example the eviction window is size 6. That equals the 2 DRAM "cache use" slots plus 4 disk slots and leaves out the DRAM "sys use" region (KV 1 + buf), which suggests capacities are counted net of system-reserved memory.

The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv. When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted."

checks.claim: 1. CA saves KV caches for all requests in a host DRAM + SSD hierarchy (AttentionStore) instead of discarding them. It fetches them back when the same session is activated again.
checks.correction: The statement is right. Two caveats: (a) 'saved' does not mean kept forever. When the disks are full, items are evicted out of AttentionStore (§3.3.2), and in §4.3.6 each session's KV has a TTL ('maximum saving time since the last access'; set to one hour in the experiment). (b) Saving is per session and happens when the session goes inactive. The KV is written asynchronously, layer by layer, during prefill and decode (§3.2.2). The wording is the same in the ATC'24 version and arXiv v3; v1 called the whole system 'AttentionStore'.
checks.quote: Abstract: "CachedAttention maintains a hierarchical KV caching system that leverages cost-effective memory/storage mediums to save KV caches for all requests." §3.1: "when the associated conversation session is inactive, CachedAttention saves the KV cache in a KV caching system, named AttentionStore, instead of discarding them as in the conventional attention mechanism. If the same conversation session is activated in the future, its KV cache is fetched from AttentionStore and reused for inference." §3.1: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." §3.3: "The access speed of host memory, i.e., DRAM, is much higher than disks, i.e., SSDs, (tens of GB/s v.s. several GB/s)."

checks.claim: 2. In CA, HBM is not a cross-turn cache tier. It holds the execution buffer plus reserved read and write buffers, and HBM-only retention (LMDeploy, RadixAttention) is treated as prior work or a baseline.
checks.correction: The substance is right, but the paper never says in so many words that HBM is not a cache tier. That follows from three things: AttentionStore is defined as host memory plus disks, §3.2.2 says cross-turn reuse comes from saving to host memory, and §4.3.7 contrasts 'caching KVs on HBMs' with 'CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs'. On baselines: the main evaluation baseline is RE (recomputation). HBM-only and HBM+DRAM appear only as comparison configurations in §4.3.7 (10GB HBM cache, cites [18,28,63], i.e. LMDeploy, FasterTransformer, SGLang). In §5, RadixAttention is called work 'developed concurrently' and is described as prefix sharing. The intro, however, groups [18,63] as 'prior works' that keep KV in HBM.

However, this quickly exhausts the limited HBM capacity." §3.2.1: "the corresponding KV cache of the layer is already in the HBM execution buffer" ... "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap." §3.2.2: "CachedAttention needs to save KV caches to host memory to enable the reuse of the KV caches across conversations." ... "we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching." §4.3.7: "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs." §4.1: "Baseline. We compare CachedAttention (CA) with re-computation (RE)." §5: "LMDeploy [18] is an LLM inference framework that caches the KV caches of multi-turn conversations on HBMs. RadixAttention [63], ChunkAttention [56], and Pensieve [58] are inference techniques that were developed concurrently with CachedAttention."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §3.2.1; §3.2.2; §4.1 Baseline; §4.3.7 Impact of Caching Storage Mediums; §5 Related Work

checks.claim: 3. CA's disk->DRAM prefetch applies only to waiting jobs in the scheduler's job queue. They must lie within a head-anchored look-ahead prefetching window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs.
checks.correction: Right in substance, with three caveats. (a) 'Head-anchored' comes from Figure 9 and its worked example, not the main text. The figure draws the prefetching window (size 2) over Jobs 2-3, next to the 'head' label, while Job 1 runs. The prose never uses the word 'head' for this window. (b) Cmem here is 'the available memory capacity for prefetching', not total DRAM. In Fig. 9 it is the 2 DRAM 'cache use' slots ('the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching'). (c) The paper never literally says 'only'. But the one prefetch trigger it describes is a waiting job inside the window whose KV is on disk. Nothing prefetches for sessions whose next turn has not yet arrived.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." Example: "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3." Figure 9 labels: "prefetching window, size: 2", "head".
