checks.claim: 4. CA's windows are counted in jobs and sized by capacity, using the average per-session KV size Skv. They contain no time, disk-bandwidth or read-backlog term.
checks.correction: Right. Both window formulas are pure capacity divided by Skv, laid over the job queue, with no time, bandwidth or backlog term. Two clarifications: the eviction window length is described as a 'maximum length'. And the paper does use a bandwidth-based sizing formula elsewhere, but only for the HBM pre-loading read buffer (§3.2.1, Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew), where B is PCIe bandwidth). That formula is not used for the disk/DRAM windows.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." §3.3.2: "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv." (Contrast, §3.2.1: "Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(TloadLhist −Tpref Lnew).")
checks.section: §3.3.1; §3.3.2; (§3.2.1 for the only bandwidth-based sizing, which is for the HBM read buffer)

checks.claim: 5. CA's look-ahead eviction window is (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long. An item whose job is inside it is exempt from eviction out of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: Right. One wording point: the paper gives (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv as the window's 'maximum length', set by AttentionStore's total capacity. In Fig. 9 the window is 6 jobs (Jobs 2-7), which equals 2 DRAM cache slots plus 4 disk slots. Job 9, the most recent arrival, is outside the window and is the one evicted out of the disk tier. The exemption applies to eviction out of AttentionStore. DRAM->disk demotion uses tail priority instead (see statement 6).
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "Specifically, CachedAttention maintains a look-ahead eviction window in the job queue. The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv. When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted." Example: "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 6. For DRAM->disk demotion, CA evicts the item nearest the tail of the look-ahead eviction window first, scanning from tail to head.
checks.correction: The tail-first rule is stated, but the statement leaves out a step and makes the rule sound stricter than the paper does. (a) In the worked example, CA first checks whether every DRAM-resident KV has an associated job in the job queue. Only because they all do does it 'then' scan tail to head. This implies that a DRAM item with no queued job (or one outside the window) would be the first victim; the paper does not spell out that case. (b) The general rule is phrased as priority: the item at the tail 'has a higher priority to be evicted'. It is not stated as a strict ordering. Also, one item is a whole session's KV, which is the minimum granularity for both eviction and fetching.
checks.quote: §3.3.2: "When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted. Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention." Example: "CachedAttention employs a look-ahead eviction window of size 6 to monitor the KV cache status of the jobs. First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: The paper does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched.
checks.correction: Confirmed silent in arXiv v1, v2 and v3 and in the USENIX ATC'24 PDF. The fetch rule only says the prefetch happens 'before these waiting jobs are executed'. No text covers a fetch that is late or still running when the job is dispatched: no stall, no direct disk-to-HBM path, no recompute fallback. The paper does give two indirect hints. KV that is on disk at access time causes 'poor inference performance'. Disk hits also count as hits in the hit-rate figures (Fig. 13, Fig. 21; CA has 'over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM', so about 0.4% are disk hits). That means disk-resident KV is still reused on some path. However, §3.2.1 describes loading into HBM only 'from the host memory', and the disk-hit path is never described.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." §2.4 (Challenge 3): "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks when being accessed, resulting in poor inference performance." §4.3.3: "CA achieves a cache hit rate of up to 86%, with over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM due to its scheduler-aware policy."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §2.4; §3.2.1; §4.2 (Fig. 13); §4.3.3

checks.claim: Because CachedAttention fetches only for jobs already in the queue, a fetch's lead time is bounded by the job's queueing delay (an inference from the fetch rule, not stated in the paper).
checks.correction: The statement is labeled correctly as an inference: the paper never states a lead-time bound. The premise holds. The only prefetch trigger the paper describes is a look-ahead window over waiting jobs in the scheduler's queue, and there is no prediction of future turns before the request arrives. The paper does not literally say 'only'. The bound is actually tighter than queueing delay. A fetch can start only once the job is within the first Lpw = Cmem/Skv waiting positions, not when it enters the queue. So lead time is at most the time the job spends inside the prefetch window, and that is no more than its queueing delay.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory (and Fig. 9)

checks.claim: The paper treats conversation requests as arriving randomly.
checks.correction: Stated verbatim three times (§1, §2.4, §3.3.1) and used as the reason that most KV caches are on disk when accessed. In the evaluation, arrivals are modeled with a Poisson process: 'sessions arriving per second', λ = 1.0, and §4.3.8 varies the session rate from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. The paper does not say how the timing of later turns within a session (the inter-turn gap) is generated. It notes that ShareGPT has no timestamps.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks, resulting in poor access performance." §4.1: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0)."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §2.4 (Challenge 3); §3.3.1; §4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads)

checks.claim: CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads its job queue; execution from the queue head in arrival order is implied, though FCFS is never named.
checks.correction: No version contains 'FCFS', 'first-come' or 'arrival order'. 'FIFO' appears only as a baseline eviction policy. The paper proposes no scheduling policy and only 'leverages the hints' from the scheduler's job queue. Execution from the head in arrival order is implied in three ways: Fig. 9 labels the queue 'head', next to the executing Job 1; the prefetch window covers the next waiting jobs (Jobs 2-3); and the tail is 'the last arrived Job 9'. Two minor caveats. First, Fig. 5 draws the 'Job Queue' and 'Job Scheduler' inside the 'CachedAttention Controller' box, but nothing about them is designed. Second, §4.1 says 'Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments', so jobs from the head join a running batch rather than running one at a time.
checks.quote: §3.1: "we present a scheduler-aware fetching scheme that leverages the hints from the job scheduler to prefetch KV caches to be accessed from disks to host memory." §3.3.1: "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs." §3.3.2: "It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail... Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted."

checks.claim: CachedAttention stores K and V before the positional encoding is applied and re-applies new positions at load time, so saved KV can be truncated on context overflow.
checks.correction: One detail is more precise in the paper. Under RPE the positional encoding is embedded only in Q and K (Fig. 11b), and Fig. 12 marks the re-applied position as 'Position (on key)'. V carries no positional encoding, so new positions are re-applied to the keys. The paper loosely calls this re-embedding into 'the KV caches'. Truncation happens on the saved KV (Fig. 12: pos [0:2048] to pos [0:1536]) before it is loaded into HBM, and new encodings are applied afterwards.
checks.quote: §3.4: "By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE as shown in Figure 11c, CachedAttention can store the KVs without embedded positional encodings in AttentionStore. When reusing the KVs in CachedAttention, the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings and further used for the following inference." §1: "CachedAttention decouples the positional encoding from the KV caches when saving them. It re-embeds the positional encoding into KV caches when loading them. After decoupling, truncation can be directly applied to the KV caches, thereby ensuring the reusability of the saved KV caches."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation (Figs. 11-12); §1; §3.1

checks.claim: Positional-encoding-decoupled truncation requires relative positional encoding.
checks.correction: Stated directly. The paper contrasts RPE with absolute positional encoding (APE), where encodings are added to the input, so APE models are not covered. Its 'RPE' category is the kind applied to Q and K, and it lists LLaMA, T5, Falcon, Mistral, Mixtral and Transformer-XL as examples.
checks.quote: §3.4: "To address this problem, CachedAttention enables the KV caches after truncation to be still valid via decoupling the positional encoding. CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE) [42, 44, 54]. Unlike the absolute positional encoding (APE) in which positional encodings are added to the input, RPE directly embeds the positional encodings in the query (Q) and key (K) vectors, as shown in Figure 11b."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation

checks.claim: In the evaluation, the truncation ratio is 0.5 (the earliest half of the tokens is discarded on overflow).
checks.correction: No correction needed. One scope note: the 0.5 sentence sits in the Baseline paragraph and is written about RE (recomputation). For CA, the paper does not restate the ratio in the evaluation setup. The same ratio is implied by §3.4 and the Figure 10 caption ('Context window size: 4K, truncation ratio: 2K'), which show both the baseline and CA cutting the first 2K of a 4K window. The Figure 12 example (pos [0:2048] -> KV [0:1536]) is only an illustration and is not the evaluated ratio. The sentence is the same in arXiv v1, v2 and v3 and in the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "When the historical tokens exceed the context window limitation, RE applies token truncation, same as the general LLM services [30]. For simplicity, the token truncation ratio is set to 0.5, implying that when an overflow occurs, the system will discard the earliest half of the tokens." (§4.1) Also §3.4: "As shown in Figure 10a, the context window size is 4K. Once the context window overflows, the LLM serving engines cut off the first 2K tokens of the prompt."
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Baseline paragraph); §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation / Figure 10 caption

checks.claim: Perplexity with CachedAttention's truncation is within 0.02 of recompute-based token truncation.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Two notes: (a) The text says the difference is '< 0.02', but its own Table 1 has one gap of exactly 0.02 (C4, LLaMA-7B: CA 6.96 vs TT 6.98). All other gaps are 0.01. So 'within 0.02' (at most 0.02) matches the table, and the paper's strict '<' is off by one case. CA is sometimes slightly better than TT and sometimes slightly worse. (b) Scope: PPL was measured only on LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-13B with WikiText-2, PTB and C4. These are not the end-to-end models (13B/65B/70B/Falcon-40B). Naive KV truncation (NKVT) gives PPL above 1000. TT is defined as removing historical tokens and recomputing the KV for the remaining tokens, so 'recompute-based token truncation' is a fair description.
checks.quote: "TT consistently achieves a low PPL by recomputing KV caches after context window overflow. CA also maintains a low PPL, comparable to TT (with a difference of< 0.02), by incorporating new positional encodings into the KV caches after truncation." checks.section: §4.3.5 Accuracy of Decoupled Positional Encoding, Table 1

checks.claim: Compared with the OF baseline (positions embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache), CachedAttention's hit rates are higher by 17.6 / 41.5 / 18.1 / 18.4 points for LLaMA-13B / 65B / 70B / Falcon-40B.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The text writes the numbers as '%' and frames them as OF's hit rates decreasing compared with CA, which leaves open whether they are relative or absolute. I measured the bars in Figure 22a by pixel height (rendered at 400 dpi). CA is about 86 / 71.5 / 88.5 / 90.5 and OF is about 68 / 30 / 70.5 / 72, which gives gaps of about 17.5 / 41.7 / 17.9 / 18.0. That confirms absolute percentage points. A relative reading would put OF for 65B near 41.5%, and the bar shows about 30%. Setup: 128GB DRAM plus 10TB SSD. The large 65B gap comes from LLaMA-1-65B's 2K context window. Version caveat: arXiv v1 reported different numbers ('hit rates decrease by 52%, 56%, 57%, 48%'). The 17.6/41.5/18.1/18.4 figures are in v2, v3 and the ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "we compare a baseline approach overflow (OF) that embeds positional encoding within the KV caches, leading to the invalidation of KV caches in AttentionStore. OF relegates context overflow to be managed by recomputation. This experiment uses 128GB DRAM and 10TB SSD. As evident from Figure 22a, comparing OF with CA, the hit rates decrease by 17.6%, 41.5%, 18.1%, 18.4% for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B, and Falcon-40B, respectively." ... "OF of LLaMA-65B experiences a low hit rate due to its limited 2K context window."
checks.section: §4.3.4 Performance of Decoupled KV Cache Truncation, Figure 22a

checks.correction: No correction needed. The paper calls it a 'token discarding list (TDL)'. TDL appears only in §3.4. The evaluation never mentions TDL or KV compression: §4.3.4 compares OF and CA, and §4.3.5 compares CA, TT and NKVT only. 'Compression' otherwise appears only in Related Work, which calls those techniques 'orthogonal', and in the references. Version note: the TDL paragraph is in arXiv v3 and the ATC'24 PDF but not in v1 or v2 (then titled 'AttentionStore').
checks.quote: "Note that CachedAttention also allows for selective preservation of certain KV cache for compression, e.g., the initial tokens with important scores [54] or important tokens [12,24,61], to further improve the generation quality of LLMs. Specifically, a given KV cache compression technique essentially provides a methodology for creating a token discarding list (TDL), in the prompt, e.g., discarding the least important tokens. CachedAttention straightforwardly complies with the TDL, discarding the KV cache associated with the TDL within the AttentionStore. After discarding the selected KV caches, AttentionStore delivers the pruned KV cache to the inference engine upon an inference execution."
checks.section: §3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation (no matching evaluation in §4)

Thus the total number of conversation turns is about 52K. We warm up AttentionStore using the first 10K conversation turns and then evaluate the performance on the following 42K turns."
checks.section: §4.2 End-to-end Performance (also §4.1 Workloads: "9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments.")

checks.claim: Session arrivals are generated from a Poisson distribution with λ = 1.0 sessions/s, and §4.3.8 sweeps 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The unit 'sessions/s' comes from the wording 'number of different sessions arriving per second'. The §4.3.8 sweep covers only LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB, and hit rate falls from 82% to 77% as the rate rises from 0.5 to 2.0. Relevant to the comparison with your design: the paper does not say how later turns within a session are timed. It gives no inter-turn or think-time model and no per-session gap distribution, only the session-level Poisson rate. Its fetching and eviction rely on look-ahead windows over the scheduler's job queue, not on predicting when a session's next turn will arrive. Version note: the §4.3.8 arrival-rate study exists only in v3 and the ATC'24 PDF. In v1 and v2, §4.3.8 covers other topics.
checks.quote: "As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (§4.1) and "In the experiments, we configure the session arrival rates varying from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. We test LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB storage following warmup as before." (§4.3.8)
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads); §4.3.8 Impact of Session Arrival Rates

checks.claim: CachedAttention describes a token-discarding-list (TDL) hook for KV compression methods, but does not evaluate it.
checks.correction: This holds. The only nuance is the word 'hook', which is ours, not the paper's. The paper says an external KV-compression technique 'provides' a TDL and that CachedAttention 'straightforwardly complies' with it by dropping the matching KV entries in AttentionStore before handing the pruned cache to the engine. The paper never says how this connects to the compression method in practice. No evaluation subsection (4.2, 4.3.1-4.3.8) tests TDL-based or importance-based compression. Sections 4.3.4 and 4.3.5 evaluate only contiguous prefix truncation when the context window overflows (decoupled positional encoding vs. OF/TT/NKVT). The only other mention of compression is Related Work, which calls quantization and compression techniques 'orthogonal to CachedAttention'. Checked against arXiv v3 (last revised 30 Jun 2024) and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF; the TDL text is the same in both.

CachedAttention straightforwardly complies with the TDL, discarding the KV cache associated with the TDL within the AttentionStore. After discarding the selected KV caches, AttentionStore delivers the pruned KV cache to the inference engine upon an inference execution." (Sec. 3.4). Evaluation covers only truncation: "We evaluate the impact of the different schemes including CA, token truncation (TT), and naive KV cache truncation (NKVT) on the perplexity (PPL) and the accuracy of LLMs" (Sec. 4.3.5). checks.claim: CachedAttention generates session arrivals with a Poisson process (λ = 1.0 sessions/s by default, swept from 0.5 to 2.0 sessions/s) on ShareGPT conversations, because the dataset has no arrival timestamps.
checks.correction: Every part is stated in the paper: the ShareGPT source, the missing timestamps as the reason, Poisson arrivals, λ = 1.0 sessions/s, and the 0.5-2.0/s sweep. Three qualifications. (1) The sweep (Sec. 4.3.8) uses only LLaMA-13B with 128GB DRAM / 10TB SSD; the other models run only at λ = 1.0. (2) The Figure 25 x-axis ticks go up to 2.5, but the text says the sweep is 0.5/s to 2.0/s. (3) The paper gives Poisson arrivals only for sessions. It never says how the later turns of a session are timed (no think-time, inter-turn gap or reply-delay model), so the gap between a session's turns in their workload is unknown. That matters when comparing against a design that predicts each session's next admission time. Other details: 9K ShareGPT sessions, 5.75 turns on average, about 52K turns, the first 10K turns used for warmup, and the Poisson method described as 'following prior works [21,52]'. Same text in arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "Workloads. The workload is integrated from the ShareGPT dataset [33, 62]. As there is no public request arrival timestamp available in the dataset, we generate request arrival times based on the Poisson distribution with various arrival rates, following prior works [21,52]. We set the number of different sessions arriving per second according to a Poisson distribution (with λ = 1.0). 9K conversation sessions are used in the experiments." (Sec. 4.1). "In the experiments, we configure the session arrival rates varying from 0.5/s to 2.0/s. We test LLaMA-13B with 128GB/10TB storage following warmup as before." (Sec. 4.3.8)
checks.section: 4.1 Experimental Setup (Workloads); 4.3.8 Impact of Session Arrival Rates (Figure 25)

checks.claim: 1. Both windows are counted in jobs, sized by capacity, and take no account of time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
checks.correction: Supported, with three caveats. (a) Both windows sit on the job queue. Their lengths are capacity divided by the average KV size of one session (Skv), so a window is a number of job slots estimated from that average, not an exact count of bytes. (b) The paper calls (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv the *maximum* length of the eviction window. (c) The 'no time, bandwidth or backlog' part is true because nothing is there: neither formula has such a term, and the paper never discusses one for the windows. Disk bandwidth appears only in the §2 motivation ('the disks have an access bandwidth of less than 5 GB/s'). PCIe bandwidth B appears only in the §3.2.1 HBM read-buffer size, Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew), which is unrelated to the prefetch and eviction windows. The wording is the same in arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." ... "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: 2. Nothing is prefetched for a session that has no job in the queue.
checks.correction: The paper implies this but never says it outright. The only prefetch trigger it describes is a waiting job inside the look-ahead prefetching window, and no other disk-to-DRAM prefetch path exists. The real rule is narrower than the claim: only jobs in the first Lpw = Cmem/Skv queue positions are prefetched. In Fig. 9 only Jobs 2–3 are checked and only KV 3 is fetched. The intro says the scheme 'pre-fetches the KV caches that are likely to be accessed... by utilizing the hints received from the inference job scheduler'. There is no prediction for sessions without a queued job.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory (also Fig. 9 walkthrough)

checks.claim: 3. An item whose job is inside the look-ahead eviction window is exempt from being evicted out of AttentionStore.
checks.correction: Matches the text, with one scope note. The exemption covers only eviction *out of AttentionStore* (dropping from disk). It does not cover host-to-disk demotion, which can still pick items inside the window, as Job 4 shows in Fig. 9. One item is all the KV of one conversation session.
checks.quote: "When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks

checks.claim: 4. For host-to-disk demotion, the item at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has the highest priority to be evicted (the scan runs tail to head).
checks.correction: The tail-to-head scan and tail-first preference are stated. 'Highest' overstates it in two ways. (1) The general rule uses the comparative 'higher priority'. (2) In the Fig. 9 walkthrough, the scan runs only after a first check of whether every host-memory KV has an associated job in the queue. That implies a host-resident KV with no queued job would be considered before the tail scan, though the paper never spells out that branch. So tail-of-window comes first only among host-resident KVs whose jobs are in the window. The paper also says nothing about host-resident KVs whose jobs are queued beyond the window. In Fig. 9 the victim is Job 4, third of six in the window. It is chosen because it is the host-resident KV nearest the tail: KV 7 is already on disk, and no KV 5 or KV 6 appears in DRAM.
checks.quote: "When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted." ... "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. Therefore, the KV cache for Job 4 is selected to be evicted from the host memory to the disks."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 5. In the paper's Fig. 9 example, when the disk is full, the KV of the last-arrived queued job outside the size-6 window (Job 9) is dropped out of the system.
checks.correction: Confirmed by the text and the figure together. Fig. 9 draws the 'eviction window, size: 6' brace over Job 2 to Job 7, so Jobs 8 and 9 lie outside it. 'Outside the window' comes from the figure, not the prose. KV 9 sits on disk with an arrow leaving the disks box, and KV 4 takes its place. The prose says 'most suitable candidate to be evicted'. 'Out of the system' follows from the general rule that a full disk evicts KVs 'out of the system'. Job 9 is still in the queue, so the KV of a queued job outside the window is dropped. Among the two jobs outside the window (8 and 9), the last-arrived one is chosen.
checks.quote: "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted. Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9." (and earlier: "if the disks are full, we also need to evict some KV caches stored in the disks out of the system.")
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 6. The paper does not specify the eviction order among cached sessions that have no queued job.
checks.correction: Correct. No ordering rule (LRU, FIFO, size or anything else) is given for sessions without a queued job. LRU and FIFO appear only as baselines. Two nearby facts are worth knowing. (a) The Fig. 9 walkthrough first checks whether host-memory KVs all have a queued job, which implies such sessions are demoted ahead of queued ones, with no tie-break among them. (b) §4.3.6 gives each session's KV a TTL, a maximum saving time since last access, set to one hour in that experiment. TTL is time-based expiry, not an eviction order under capacity pressure.
checks.quote: "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue." (§3.3.2) ... "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above." ... "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour." (§4.3.6)
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement

checks.claim: CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer so pre-loading can start while the previous job is still running, and sizes it as Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew); imperfect overlap occurs when Tload·Lhist > Tpref·Lnew.
checks.correction: Matches the paper. One nuance: the paper introduces the buffer in two steps. First, a read buffer closes the gap between jobs. Second, a 'customized larger pre-loading buffer' covers imperfect overlap, and the Sbuf formula sizes this larger buffer (B = PCIe bandwidth; Tload and Tpref are per-token load and prefill times). The evaluation treats both as one read buffer of varying size (PL-B0 to PL-B15). Wording is identical in arXiv v3 (30 Jun 2024), USENIX ATC'24 and v1.

Specifically, as shown in Figure 6c, with the read buffer, the read stream doesn't have to wait for the release of the execution buffer from the last job. The read stream can start the pre-loading while the last job is running." ... "The overhead can be further minimized by employing a customized larger pre-loading buffer." ... "Imperfect overlapping happens when Tload Lhist > Tpref Lnew, which indicates that the transmission time is larger than the partial prefilling time. The buffer is used to fill up the time gap Tload Lhist − Tpref Lnew. Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: Sbuf = B(Tload Lhist − Tpref Lnew)."
checks.section: §3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs (Figures 6c, 7b)

checks.claim: In CachedAttention's micro-benchmark (LLaMA-13B, 1K history + 100 new tokens), layer-wise pre-loading without a read buffer (PL-B0) reduced prefill time by 35%, and with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15) by 61%.
checks.correction: Correct. Both reductions are measured against NO-PL (no pre-loading, which counts KV load time plus compute time). The setup is LLaMA-13B on a single GPU with batch size 16. The text writes 'PF-B15' (a typo), while the Figure 19 axis label is PL-B15. The paper says PL-B15 'perfectly overlaps' the load time.
checks.quote: "The model used is LLaMA-13B with a single GPU and the batch size is set to 16. Layer-wise KV cache pre-loading. We set the length of historical tokens to 1K and the length of newly input tokens to 100 ... e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache. We observe although there is no read buffer, i.e., PL-B0, the pre-loading scheme reduces the prefilling time by 35% compared to NO-PL. PF-B15 perfectly overlaps the KV cache loading time and reduces the prefilling time by 61% compared to NO-PL."
checks.section: §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access (Figure 19)

checks.claim: CachedAttention saves KV from HBM to host memory asynchronously: prefill KV is written layer by layer and overlapped with decoding, decode KV is written layer by layer while decoding, and unfinished writes go to a reserved HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked.
checks.correction: Correct. Minor wording point: for prefill, the paper says the write stream 'retains' the KV cache layer by layer and that this KV 'can be overlapped with the decoding phase'. It does not literally say 'written'. Figure 8b shows the prefill KV being written during decode.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention needs to save KV caches to host memory to enable the reuse of the KV caches across conversations." ... "for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding. To avoid getting stuck if the KV cached is not fully written back when the decoding is already finished, we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job."
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory (Figure 8)

checks.claim: CachedAttention rejects writing all KV after the turn ends because the saving time would be on the critical path, and reports that asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15%.
checks.correction: Correct. 'Rejects' is a fair paraphrase: the paper calls end-of-turn writing the 'baseline method' and says it 'potentially delays' the next jobs. The 13-15% cut is in 'overall execution time'. It comes from a micro-benchmark: LLaMA-13B, single GPU, batch 16, prompt lengths 1K to 1.6K, 20 decoding steps. It is not an end-to-end result.
checks.quote: "A baseline method to save the KV caches is to write all produced KV caches together after the round of conversation ends. This method however potentially delays the execution of the next scheduled jobs since the KV saving time is on the critical path of inference, as shown in Figure 8a." ... "We set different prompt lengths ranging from 1K to 1.6K and the number of decoding steps to 20 ... CachedAttention employs the asynchronous saving scheme allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution, reducing the overall execution time by 13% to 15%."
checks.section: §3.2.2 (Figure 8a) and §4.3.2 Asynchronous KV cache saving (Figure 20)

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, HBM holds the execution buffer plus read and write buffers and is not used as a cross-turn cache tier; keeping KV in HBM only is evaluated as a baseline.
checks.correction: Supported, with caveats. (a) The paper names the HBM execution, read and write buffers, but it never lists everything HBM holds. The exclusion of HBM is drawn from how it defines AttentionStore (host memory and disks) and from §4.3.7, which contrasts 'caching KVs on HBMs' with 'CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs'. There is no explicit rule such as 'HBM is not a tier'. (b) One intro sentence leaves a small opening: previous jobs' KV is moved out of HBM 'if the HBM space is not enough'. The paper never describes reusing HBM-resident KV across turns. (c) There are two baselines, not one: HBM-only (a 10GB HBM cache) and HBM+DRAM. Their hit rates are about 0% and 1.7-19.1%; CA reaches 71-90%.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention employs multi-tier cost-effective storage mediums in AttentionStore, i.e., host memory and disks." (§3.1) ... "Some existing works [18,28,63] employ only the HBM space for caching the KV caches of multi-turn conversations. We here compare the performance of mechanism caching KVs on HBMs with that of CachedAttention caching KVs on DRAM and SSDs. In the experiments, we configure the size of the HBM cache as 10GB, the size of DRAM as 128GB, and the size of SSDs as 10TB ... The hit rate of the HBM-only caching method is nearly 0% for all models due to the limited capacity of HBM. Using HBM with DRAM improves the cache hit rate to 3.4%, 1.7%, 7.7%, and 19.1%" (§4.3.7). Caveat from §1: "the subsequent inference jobs need to wait until the KV caches from the previous jobs are moved out of the HBMs if the HBM space is not enough."
checks.section: §3.1 Overview (Figure 5), §3.2.1/§3.2.2 (HBM execution/read/write buffers), §4.3.7 Impact of Caching Storage Mediums (Figure 24), §1

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, KV reaches disk by eviction (demotion) from host memory, triggered when free host memory reaches a threshold whose value is not given, not by write-through.
checks.correction: Correct in substance. The paper never uses the words 'write-through' or 'demotion'. 'Not by write-through' is inferred: saving targets host memory only, and disks are reached only through eviction or migration from host memory. The trigger is described two ways. §3.3.1 says 'a defined threshold' and gives no value anywhere. §3.3.2 says 'when the free space in the host memory is exhausted'. Eviction moves the whole session's KV as one item. Victims are chosen from the tail of a look-ahead window over the job queue, and the scheme can also evict out of the system when disks are full.
checks.quote: "Note that CachedAttention includes a host memory buffer that allows for seamless fetching of KV caches from disks to memory, preventing any delays when the host memory is full. When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold, CachedAttention triggers a KV eviction from host memory to disks to ensure the constant availability of the host memory buffer." (§3.3.1) ... "When the free space in the host memory is exhausted, we need to evict some KV caches from the host memory to disks. Meanwhile, if the disks are full, we also need to evict some KV caches stored in the disks out of the system." (§3.3.2)
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; §3.2.2 (save target is host memory)

checks.claim: 1. CachedAttention moves data between GPU and host on dedicated CUDA streams and between host memory and disks on separate IO threads.
checks.correction: Accurate as stated. The sentence comes from the implementation paragraph of the experimental setup (§4.1), not from the design sections. §3.2 also names a 'read stream', an 'execution stream' and a 'write stream' for layer-wise pre-loading and asynchronous saving, and §3.3.1 refers to 'KV cache fetching threads' for disk-to-memory prefetch. The arXiv v3 text (revised 30 Jun 2024) and the USENIX ATC '24 PDF are identical here.
checks.quote: "Dedicated CUDA streams are used for moving data between the GPUs and the host memory, overlapping the computation with proactive swapping. Separate IO threads migrate data between the host memory and the disks, overlapping the execution with the KV cache migrations."
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (Testbeds / implementation paragraph); see also §3.3.1: "Then the KV cache fetching threads start fetching the KV cache for Job 3 from disks to the host memory."

checks.claim: 2. CachedAttention prefetches KV from disk to host memory only for jobs already in the scheduler's queue, within a look-ahead window of Lpw = Cmem/Skv jobs; nothing is fetched for a session with no queued job.
checks.correction: The mechanism and formula are verbatim. Prefetch looks at waiting jobs in the job queue through a look-ahead window of length Lpw = Cmem/Skv. Cmem is 'the available memory capacity for prefetching', not total host memory, and Skv is 'the average KV size of a session'. The paper never actually says 'only', and it never says that nothing is fetched for a session with no queued job. The queue is simply the only prefetch trigger it describes, so the exclusivity is an inference from silence, not a stated rule. The paper also does not say what happens when a job reaches execution while its KV is still on disk (an on-demand load).
checks.quote: "Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory (and Figure 9)

checks.claim: 3. CachedAttention does not predict when a session's next turn will arrive and does not model think time between turns; the paper says that because conversation requests arrive randomly, their KV caches are more likely to be on disk when accessed.
checks.correction: The quoted reasoning appears nearly word for word in three places: the Introduction, §2.4 Challenge 3 and §3.3.1. The paper never mentions predicting next-turn arrival, think time or inter-turn gaps. Its only source of 'future access information' is the job queue. The closest thing to a timing mechanism is a per-session TTL, a maximum saving time since last access (§4.3.6, set to one hour in the capacity experiment). That is a retention bound, not a prediction. The workload section describes only Poisson session arrivals (λ = 1.0 sessions/s) and does not say how turns inside a session are spaced.
checks.quote: §2.4: "As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks when being accessed, resulting in poor inference performance. It is essential to ensure that the KV cache to be accessed in the immediate future is always placed in the host memory instead of disks." §3.3.2: "CachedAttention presents a scheduler-aware eviction scheme which can leverage the future access information of KV caches to achieve a higher cache hit rate. The job queue in the job scheduler gives us the opportunity to achieve this."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §2.4 Challenge 3 'Suitable placement of KV caches in different hierarchies'; §3.3.1; §3.3.2; §4.1 Workloads; §4.3.6 (TTL)

checks.claim: 4. CachedAttention's look-ahead eviction window, (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv jobs long, exempts items whose job lies in the window from being evicted out of AttentionStore, and when demoting from host memory to disks it gives priority to items near the window's tail.
checks.correction: Accurate. Precisely, (Cmem+Cdisk)/Skv is the window's maximum length, set by AttentionStore's total capacity. The exemption is stated only for eviction out of AttentionStore. For memory-to-disk eviction the paper says only that the tail item 'has a higher priority'. In the Figure 9 example, the window is scanned 'from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail'.
checks.quote: "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem + Cdisk)/Skv. When CachedAttention attempts to evict one item out of AttentionStore, if finding the item to be evicted in the look-ahead eviction window, the item is exempted. When CachedAttention evicts one item from the host memory to disks, the item located at the tail of the look-ahead eviction window has a higher priority to be evicted."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks (and Figure 9 example)

checks.claim: 5. CachedAttention does not specify the eviction order among cached sessions that have no queued job.
checks.correction: Correct: the paper gives no ordering, such as LRU or FIFO, among cached sessions with no associated queued job. Two nuances apply. (a) The Figure 9 walkthrough implies, without saying so, that such sessions are evicted before any windowed one: the scheduler first checks whether all host-memory caches have a queued job, and only then scans the window from tail to head. (b) Each session's KV has a TTL measured from its last access (§4.3.6), which bounds how long it is retained but does not define a capacity-eviction order. LRU and FIFO appear only as baselines in §4.3.3.
checks.quote: §3.3.2 example: "First, it finds that the KV caches in the host memory all have an associated job in the job queue. It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail." §4.3.6: "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access."
checks.section: §3.3.2 (Figure 9 example); §4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement; §4.3.3 (LRU/FIFO used only as baselines)

checks.claim: 6. CachedAttention's minimal eviction and fetching granularity is one item holding all the KV of a conversation session, because a session's KV is either all used or none of it is used.
checks.correction: Accurate, almost verbatim. Physical storage is still allocated in blocks: §4.1 says 'The host memory and disks are managed in the form of blocks to improve storage utilization, similar to [21].' Allocation is block-based, but eviction and fetch work on whole sessions.
checks.quote: "Note that one item corresponds to all KV caches associated with a conversation session, which is the minimal eviction and fetching granularity in CachedAttention. This is because the KV cache in the same conversation session is either all used or none of it is used."
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; block allocation in §4.1

checks.claim: 1. CA states that because conversation requests arrive randomly, their KV caches are more likely to be on disk when accessed.
checks.correction: No correction needed. The paper states this three times (§1, §2.4 Challenge 3, §3.3.1), and the §2.4 wording includes 'when being accessed'. The claim rests on a capacity premise: disks are much larger than DRAM, so 'most KV caches are retained in disks'. The paper asserts this and does not measure it. Version note: arXiv v3 (30 Jun 2024) and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF have identical text. In v1/v2 (titled 'AttentionStore: ...') the sentence is the same except the system is called AttentionStore.
checks.quote: "Disks provide much larger capacity than the host memory (tens of TBs v.s. several hundreds of GBs). Thus most KV caches are retained in disks. However, the disks have an access bandwidth of less than 5 GB/s. As conversation requests arrive randomly, their corresponding KV caches are more likely to be located in disks when being accessed, resulting in poor inference performance. It is essential to ensure that the KV cache to be accessed in the immediate future is always placed in the host memory instead of disks."
checks.section: §2.4 Opportunities and Challenges, item 3 'Suitable placement of KV caches in different hierarchies' (same idea in §1 Introduction and §3.3.1); arXiv v3 = USENIX ATC'24 p.4

checks.claim: 2. (Stated as the user's own inference, not the paper's) Because CA fetches only for queued jobs, its disk-fetch lead time is bounded by each job's queueing delay.
checks.correction: The paper never discusses lead time or queueing delay, so the bound itself cannot be checked against it. The premise is supported: the only disk-to-DRAM fetch trigger described is waiting jobs inside the look-ahead prefetching window. The inference holds, but the real bound is tighter. A job can only be prefetched once it is within the first L_pw = C_mem/S_kv waiting positions (Figure 9 shows the window covering the two jobs right behind the executing one). So lead time <= time spent inside that window <= total queueing delay. Two more points from the paper. (a) KV is saved to host memory after a turn (§3.2.2) and stays there until evicted, so a returning session can hit DRAM with no fetch at all. The bound only applies to sessions already demoted to disk. (b) The paper gives no measurement of how timely prefetches are. It only reports that 'over 99.6% of the hits occurring in DRAM' (§4.3.3) under its Poisson λ=1.0 sessions/s workload, which suggests the window gave enough lead time in that setup.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed. The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching C_mem and the average KV size of a session S_kv, the prefetching window length is L_pw = C_mem/S_kv." ... "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory and Figure 9; context from §3.2.2 and §4.3.3

checks.claim: 3. CA does not modify the scheduler. It reads the job queue, whose head and tail imply FCFS execution, and it does not reorder jobs by cache location.
checks.correction: 'Reads the job queue' is accurate: CA uses the queue as 'hints'. 'Head and tail imply FCFS' is a fair inference but not a stated fact. The queue is in arrival order (the tail item is 'the last arrived Job 9'), but the paper never names a scheduling policy. The only scheduling detail in the evaluation is that continuous batching is enabled. 'Does not modify the scheduler' is not stated anywhere. Figure 5 actually draws the Job Scheduler and Job Queue inside the 'CachedAttention Controller' box, next to the AttentionStore Manager. 'Does not reorder jobs by cache location' rests on silence: no reordering is described, but no reordering is explicitly ruled out either. Safer wording: 'The CA paper only uses the job queue as a hint source for prefetch and eviction. It describes no cache-aware reordering and names no policy beyond an arrival-ordered queue.'
checks.quote: §1: "This scheme pre-fetches the KV caches that are likely to be accessed from disks to the host memory, by utilizing the hints received from the inference job scheduler." §3.3.1: "the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs." §3.3.2: "It then proceeds to scan the look-ahead eviction window from tail to head, prioritizing the eviction of jobs near the tail. ... the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted." Figure 5 (drawing): box labelled "CachedAttention Controller" contains "Job Scheduler" (with "Job Queue") and "AttentionStore Manager". §4.1: "Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments."
checks.section: §1 Introduction; §3.3.1; §3.3.2; Figure 5 (system architecture); §4.1 Experimental Setup

checks.claim: 4. CA does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or mid-fetch.
checks.correction: Accurate: the paper is silent on this case. The nearest passages cover other situations. (a) The host memory buffer is said to prevent delays 'when the host memory is full', which is a different case from an unfinished fetch. (b) The Introduction says in general that a job cannot compute before its KV is in HBM, but does not say whether the job stalls, is skipped, or is recomputed. (c) §3.2.1 only covers loading from memory to HBM; no path from disk to HBM is described. (d) §4.2 counts 'disk hit rates', so disk-resident hits do happen, but how they are served is never explained. §4.3.3 reports that over 99.6% of hits were in DRAM, so the case was rare in their evaluation.
checks.quote: §3.3.1: "Note that CachedAttention includes a host memory buffer that allows for seamless fetching of KV caches from disks to memory, preventing any delays when the host memory is full." §1: "GPUs can only perform the computation of an inference job after successfully loading its corresponding KV cache into HBMs." §4.2: "Figure 13 shows the total KV cache hit rates, including both DRAM and disk hit rates across various LLMs."
checks.section: §3.3.1 (only nearby text); §1 Introduction; §3.2.1 (memory to HBM only); §4.2 Cache hit rate; searched the full text of v1/v2/v3 and the ATC'24 PDF with no match

checks.claim: 5. CA saves KV asynchronously and layer by layer during the job. An HBM write buffer holds unfinished writes, and this cut total execution time by 13-15%.
checks.correction: The mechanism is described correctly. Saving goes from HBM to host memory, layer by layer. Prefill KV writes overlap with the decoding phase and decode KV is written back while decoding. An HBM write buffer takes unfinished KV so the next job is not blocked. The problem is the attribution: the paper credits the 13-15% cut to the asynchronous saving scheme as a whole ('allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution'), not to the write buffer. It never measures the write buffer separately. Also, 13-15% comes from a microbenchmark (LLaMA-13B, single GPU, batch 16, prompt lengths 1K-1.6K, 20 decoding steps), not an end-to-end result. Suggested wording: '...holds unfinished writes. In a microbenchmark, asynchronous saving cut total execution time by 13-15%.'
checks.quote: §3.2.2: "for the prefilling phase, as each self-attention operation can produce a significant amount of KV cache, the write stream retains the KV cache layer by layer. The KV cache produced by the prefilling phase can be overlapped with the decoding phase. For the decoding phase, as the KV cache is iteratively produced, the write stream writes back the KV cache layer by layer while decoding. To avoid getting stuck if the KV cached is not fully written back when the decoding is already finished, we also reserve an HBM write buffer to cover such cases similar to the read buffer used in the KV cache prefetching. The unfinished KV caches are temporarily moved to the write buffer to avoid blocking the execution of the next job." §4.3.2: "We set different prompt lengths ranging from 1K to 1.6K and the number of decoding steps to 20 ... CachedAttention employs the asynchronous saving scheme allowing KV cache saving to overlap with inference execution, reducing the overall execution time by 13% to 15%."
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory; §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access ('Asynchronous KV cache saving'), Figure 20

checks.claim: 6. CA overlaps layer-wise DRAM->HBM pre-loading with prefill, using an HBM read buffer sized Sbuf = B(Tload·Lhist − Tpref·Lnew). Prefill time fell 35% with no buffer (PL-B0) and 61% with a 15-layer buffer (PL-B15).
checks.correction: No substantive correction. Minor details: (a) Both reductions are relative to NO-PL (no pre-loading), measured in a microbenchmark: LLaMA-13B, single GPU, batch 16, 1K historical tokens, 100 new tokens. (b) B is 'the PCIe bandwidth'; T_load and T_pref are per-token times. (c) The read buffer has two roles. The basic buffer lets the read stream start while the previous job is still running (Fig. 6c). The formula sizes the 'customized larger pre-loading buffer' used when T_load·L_hist > T_pref·L_new (Fig. 7b). (d) The body text writes 'PF-B15', a typo; the Figure 19 label is PL-B15. Buffer sizes are given in layers of KV cache.
checks.quote: §3.2.1: "The main idea is to overlap the loading of the KV cache with the prefilling computation of new input tokens for the conversation." ... "CachedAttention reserves an HBM read buffer to eliminate the gap." ... "Imperfect overlapping happens when T_load L_hist > T_pref L_new ... The buffer is used to fill up the time gap T_load L_hist − T_pref L_new. Combined with the PCIe bandwidth B, the buffer size can be set by the following formula: S_buf = B(T_load L_hist − T_pref L_new)." §4.3.2: "we use the number of layers to represent the buffer size, e.g., PL-B0 indicates no read buffer and PF-B5 indicates a read buffer size of 5 layers of KV cache. We observe although there is no read buffer, i.e., PL-B0, the pre-loading scheme reduces the prefilling time by 35% compared to NO-PL. PF-B15 perfectly overlaps the KV cache loading time and reduces the prefilling time by 61% compared to NO-PL."
checks.section: §3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs (Figures 6-7); §4.3.2 Overlapped KV cache Access ('Layer-wise KV cache pre-loading'), Figure 19

checks.claim: In CachedAttention, KV reaches disk by demotion (eviction triggered when free host memory reaches a threshold), not by write-through.
checks.correction: Supported, with two caveats. (a) The paper never uses the term 'write-through'. The 'not write-through' part comes from the design, which describes no other path to disk. Figure 5 has only 'Save (§3.2.2)' from HBM to host memory and 'Evict (§3.3.2)' from host memory to disks; there is no HBM-to-disk arrow. Figure 9 also shows KV 4, KV 2 and KV 1 in DRAM with no disk copy, and evicting KV 4 means writing it to disk in place of KV 9. (b) The trigger is worded two ways. §3.3.1 says eviction starts when free memory 'reaches a defined threshold' so a host buffer stays free. §3.3.2 opens with 'When the free space in the host memory is exhausted'. The wording is the same in arXiv v1/v2 (which say 'AttentionStore' instead of 'CachedAttention'), v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention needs to save KV caches to host memory to enable the reuse of the KV caches across conversations." (§3.2.2) ... "When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold, CachedAttention triggers a KV eviction from host memory to disks to ensure the constant availability of the host memory buffer." (§3.3.1) ... "When the free space in the host memory is exhausted, we need to evict some KV caches from the host memory to disks." (§3.3.2)
checks.section: §3.2.2 Asynchronous Saving from HBMs to Memory; §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 5; Figure 9

checks.claim: The paper does not give the value of the host-memory threshold.
checks.correction: Confirmed. The only mention is 'a defined threshold', with no number, fraction or size, in v1, v2, v3 and the ATC'24 PDF. The related sizes are given only as formulas: prefetch window Lpw = Cmem/Skv and eviction window (Cmem + Cdisk)/Skv. The only concrete figures are the testbed sizes (128GB DRAM / 10TB SSD, plus 2T/5T SSD in §4.3.3) and the illustrative window sizes in Figure 9 (prefetch 2, eviction 6, one 'buf' slot).
checks.quote: "Note that CachedAttention includes a host memory buffer that allows for seamless fetching of KV caches from disks to memory, preventing any delays when the host memory is full. When the capacity of the free memory reaches a defined threshold, CachedAttention triggers a KV eviction from host memory to disks to ensure the constant availability of the host memory buffer."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory

checks.claim: The paper never states whether its tiers are inclusive or exclusive; its migration wording ('moved', 'migrate') suggests exclusive placement.
checks.correction: The words 'inclusive' and 'exclusive' do not appear in any version, so 'never states' holds. The paper does use 'migrated', 'moved' and 'migrate', so the wording claim holds too. For demotion there is stronger evidence than wording alone. (1) In Figure 9, KV 4, KV 2 and KV 1 are in DRAM only, and evicting KV 4 means writing it to the disk slot of Job 9. Under inclusive tiers it would already be on disk. (2) The eviction-window length (Cmem + Cdisk)/Skv adds the two capacities as if they do not overlap. For promotion (disk to DRAM) the evidence is mixed. KV 3 is 'migrated to the host memory', yet in the same example 'the disks are also full' and Job 9 must be evicted rather than KV 4 taking KV 3's old slot. This fits a kept disk copy, or simply operations running at the same time. So 'exclusive' is well supported for demotion but not established for promotion.
checks.quote: "When the KV cache of Job 3 is chosen to be migrated to the host memory, the buffer will be utilized." ... "Finally, the KV cache for Job 4 is moved to the location previously occupied by Job 9." (§3.3.2); "The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem + Cdisk)/Skv." (§3.3.2); "Separate IO threads migrate data between the host memory and the disks" (§4.1)
checks.section: §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9; §4.1 Experimental Setup

checks.claim: The paper does not say whether the disk copy is kept after a KV cache is fetched into host memory.
checks.correction: Confirmed. The text says only that KV is 'pre-fetch[ed]' or 'migrated' from disk to host memory, and never says the disk copy is freed or kept. Figure 9 shows the moment KV 3 is fetched (arrow from the disk KV 3 slot to the DRAM 'buf') but not the disk state afterwards. One detail points slightly toward the copy being kept, or at least not yet freed: while KV 3 is being migrated, the text still says 'the disks are also full' and evicts Job 9 to make room for KV 4. The Figure 9 timeline shows disks->dram KV 3 and dram->disks KV 4 at the same time, so this does not settle it. The paper is silent on this point.
checks.quote: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." (§3.3.1) ... "Since the disks are also full, the scanning process identifies that the last arrived Job 9 in the job queue is the most suitable candidate to be evicted." (§3.3.2)
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; §3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: CachedAttention uses dedicated CUDA streams for GPU-host transfers and separate IO threads for host-disk migration.
checks.correction: Stated almost word for word in the implementation paragraph of §4.1, with the same text in v1 and in the ATC'24 PDF. Related wording: §3.2 calls the GPU-side transfers the 'read stream' and 'write stream', and §3.3.1 calls the disk-to-memory readers 'KV cache fetching threads'.
checks.quote: "Dedicated CUDA streams are used for moving data between the GPUs and the host memory, overlapping the computation with proactive swapping. Separate IO threads migrate data between the host memory and the disks, overlapping the execution with the KV cache migrations."
checks.section: §4.1 Experimental Setup (implementation paragraph)

checks.claim: The paper does not specify the order in which disk reads are served.
checks.correction: The paper gives no explicit disk I/O scheduling or service order: nothing on ordering among reads in flight, among the several 'fetching threads', or for reads of KV that was not prefetched. It does say which disk reads are issued and when. Reads are prefetches for waiting jobs inside a look-ahead prefetching window at the head of the scheduler's job queue (length Lpw = Cmem/Skv), issued before those jobs run. In the example, Job 1 is running and the window covers Jobs 2-3. The queue appears to be in arrival order ('the last arrived Job 9' is at the tail). So reads go to the next jobs to execute, in job-queue order, but the order between two disk misses inside the window is not stated.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed. If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." ... "As Job 1 is executing, the KV cache manager applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3. ... Then the KV cache fetching threads start fetching the KV cache for Job 3 from disks to the host memory."
checks.section: §3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; Figure 9; §3.3.2 ("last arrived Job 9")

checks.claim: 1. CachedAttention's window lengths are derived from capacity, counted in jobs, and take no account of time, disk bandwidth or read backlog.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Two small points. (a) The paper calls the eviction-window figure a 'maximum length'. (b) The paper does use a bandwidth term in one place: the size of the separate HBM pre-loading buffer in section 3.2.1 (S_buf = B(T_load*L_hist - T_pref*L_new), where B is PCIe bandwidth). Neither window formula has a time, bandwidth or backlog term. Disk bandwidth (<5 GB/s) is mentioned only as motivation in section 2.4. The windows are counted in session KV slots and applied to positions in the job queue ('2 KV cache slots' -> 'waiting Jobs 2-3'). Checked against arXiv v3 and the USENIX ATC'24 PDF, whose text is identical.
checks.quote: "The length of the look-ahead prefetching window is determined by the available capacity in the host memory. Given the available memory capacity for prefetching Cmem and the average KV size of a session Skv, the prefetching window length is Lpw = Cmem/Skv." ... "applies a look-ahead window size of 2 (the host memory has 2 KV cache slots for the KV cache fetching) to check the KV cache hit status of the waiting Jobs 2-3." ... "The maximum length of the look-ahead eviction window is determined by the total storage capacity of AttentionStore. Assume the total available capacity in the disks is Cdisk. The look-ahead eviction window length is (Cmem +Cdisk)/Skv."
checks.section: Section 3.3.1 Scheduler-aware Fetching from Disks to Memory; Section 3.3.2 Scheduler-aware Eviction from Memory to Disks; Figure 9

checks.claim: 2. CachedAttention takes the scheduler as given and only reads its job queue; it does not reorder jobs by cache location and does not discuss preemption, priorities, SLOs or multi-instance routing.
checks.correction: No correction needed. Some details. Figure 5 draws the Job Scheduler inside a box labelled 'CachedAttention Controller', but the only arrow runs one way, from Job Scheduler to AttentionStore Manager, and the paper never describes the scheduling policy or any change to it. The word 'priority' appears only as eviction priority ('higher priority to be evicted'), never as job priority. TTFT is called a 'quality of service' metric, but no SLO is defined. Figure 5 shows a 'GPU Cluster' with GPU 0/1, but routing across instances is never discussed. Searches for preempt, SLO, deadline, route, reorder, FCFS and load balance found nothing in v1, v2, v3 or the ATC version.
checks.quote: "This is done by utilizing the hints from the inference job scheduler. Specifically, the job scheduler maintains a job queue, thus having the full knowledge of waiting jobs. CachedAttention applies a look-ahead prefetching window to watch for the waiting jobs to be executed." ... "The job queue in the job scheduler gives us the opportunity to achieve this." ... "Continuous batching [57] is enabled through experiments."
checks.section: Section 3.3.1; Section 3.3.2; Figure 5 (system architecture); Section 4.1 Experimental Setup

checks.claim: 3. CachedAttention does not say what happens when a job reaches the head of the queue while its KV is still on disk or being fetched (stall, recompute, or direct load).
checks.correction: No correction needed. The paper never describes the path for a job whose disk-to-DRAM prefetch has not finished. Layer-wise pre-loading is described only from host memory to HBM, and the fetch section only says prefetch happens 'before these waiting jobs are executed'. One indirect hint: the evaluation counts disk hits as cache hits. Figure 13 counts 'both DRAM and disk hit rates', and LRU/FIFO get '12.4% and 9.0% ... disk hit rates'. That suggests disk-resident KV is reused rather than recomputed, but the paper never states whether the job stalls, loads directly from disk, or overlaps the load.
checks.quote: "If the KV cache of the waiting jobs is hit in the disks, CachedAttention will pre-fetch the KV cache of waiting jobs from the disks to host memory before these waiting jobs are executed." ... "Note that CachedAttention includes a host memory buffer that allows for seamless fetching of KV caches from disks to memory, preventing any delays when the host memory is full." ... "CachedAttention loads KV caches from the host memory to HBMs" ... "Figure 13 shows the total KV cache hit rates, including both DRAM and disk hit rates across various LLMs."
checks.section: Section 3.3.1; Section 3.2.1 Layer-wise Pre-loading from Memory to HBMs; Section 4.2 (Cache hit rate); Section 4.3.3

checks.claim: 4. CachedAttention gives each session's KV a TTL measured from its last access, set to one hour in its capacity experiment; the paper does not say how the TTL interacts with the eviction windows.
checks.correction: No correction needed. One addition: the TTL is introduced only in the evaluation (section 4.3.6, cache-capacity analysis), not in the design (section 3). Section 3.3 never mentions it. The paper also does not say whether a TTL was active in the other experiments.
checks.quote: "In CachedAttention, the KV cache of each session has a TTL (time to live) that indicates its maximum saving time since the last access. The TTL is set as the unit time mentioned above." ... "In the experiment, we set the TTL to one hour."
checks.section: Section 4.3.6 The Cache Capacity Requirement

checks.claim: 5. CachedAttention stores K and V before the relative positional encoding is applied, so that on context overflow the stored KV can be truncated and new positions applied after loading; this requires relative positional encoding.
checks.correction: No correction needed. One clarification: the paper says RPE embeds positions only in Q and K, so V never carries a positional encoding. 'Storing before PE' therefore matters only for K. The paper's worked example truncates to KV[0:1536] before loading to HBM and then applies the new positional encodings.
checks.quote: "CachedAttention needs to work with the relative position encoding (RPE) [42, 44, 54]. Unlike the absolute positional encoding (APE) in which positional encodings are added to the input, RPE directly embeds the positional encodings in the query (Q) and key (K) vectors" ... "By simply moving the time of caching KVs before embedding positional encodings in RPE as shown in Figure 11c, CachedAttention can store the KVs without embedded positional encodings in AttentionStore. When reusing the KVs in CachedAttention, the KVs are embedded with the new positional encodings" ... "the LLM engine retrieves the truncated KV cache (i.e., KV [0:1536]) and loads it to the HBM. The new positional encodings are subsequently applied to the KV cache."
checks.section: Section 3.4 Decoupled KV Cache Truncation; Figures 11 and 12

checks.claim: 6. CachedAttention evaluates truncation with a ratio of 0.5, and its hit rate exceeded the OF baseline (positions kept embedded, so overflow invalidates the cache) by 17.6, 41.5, 18.1 and 18.4 points for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B and Falcon-40B.
checks.correction: The four numbers and the description of OF are correct. The 0.5 ratio is not stated for the truncation experiment. The paper states it only for the RE (recomputation) baseline in the section 4.1 setup. Section 4.3.4 (CA vs OF) gives no ratio, and only says it uses 128GB DRAM and 10TB SSD. Figure 10 shows a 4K window with a 2K truncation, and the Figure 12 example truncates 2048 to 1536. On 'points': the text writes 'decrease by 17.6%, ...'. The Figure 22a bars show these are absolute point gaps, not relative ones (e.g., LLaMA-65B is about 71% for CA vs about 30% for OF; LLaMA-13B is about 86% vs about 68%). The paper phrases it as OF's hit rate decreasing relative to CA.
checks.quote: Section 4.1 Baseline: "When the historical tokens exceed the context window limitation, RE applies token truncation, same as the general LLM services [30]. For simplicity, the token truncation ratio is set to 0.5, implying that when an overflow occurs, the system will discard the earliest half of the tokens." Section 4.3.4: "we compare a baseline approach overflow (OF) that embeds positional encoding within the KV caches, leading to the invalidation of KV caches in AttentionStore. OF relegates context overflow to be managed by recomputation. This experiment uses 128GB DRAM and 10TB SSD. As evident from Figure 22a, comparing OF with CA, the hit rates decrease by 17.6%, 41.5%, 18.1%, 18.4% for LLaMA-13B, LLaMA-65B, LLaMA-70B, and Falcon-40B, respectively."
